docs.title: Kafka Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Most people meet Kafka through a confusing analogy — "it's like a queue, but not really" — and never get the one idea that actually explains everything else: a Kafka topic is a durable, append-only log, split into partitions, and every consumer just remembers its own position in that log. Once that's real to you, a lot of things stop being magic: why two consumers in the same group never read the same partition, why "exactly once" needs a producer ID and a transaction coordinator and isn't free, why a compacted topic can still have old keys if you haven't read past a tombstone's retention window, and why a consumer that stops committing offsets isn't broken, it's just rewinding every time it restarts.

This course was written and run against a real, local Apache Kafka 4.4.0 broker in KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper — Kafka removed it entirely as of version 4.0) on an ordinary laptop with Java 17+. No cloud account, no managed Kafka service, and no Docker Compose cluster were needed for almost everything here: real topics, real producers and consumers, a real cgroup-free single-broker cluster, real Kafka Connect (including a genuine classpath gotcha this course hit and explains), and a real Kafka Streams application doing real stateful aggregation.

It assumes basic programming and command-line comfort. No prior messaging-system or distributed-systems experience is assumed, though if you want Java itself in depth first, see the Java Mastery Path.

docs.title: Level 1 · The Log, Topics & Partitions
docs.text:
Level 1 builds the one mental model everything else in this course depends on: a topic is a partitioned, durable, append-only log, and almost every Kafka behavior — ordering, delivery guarantees, consumer group rebalancing, replication — falls directly out of that one fact. Every command shown here was run against a real, local, single-broker Kafka cluster.

What was run, and what wasn't

This course runs a real Apache Kafka 4.4.0 broker in KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper — removed entirely as of Kafka 4.0) on a laptop, using the bundled command-line tools (kafka-topics.sh, kafka-console-producer.sh, kafka-console-consumer.sh, kafka-consumer-groups.sh). Every piece of terminal output in this level is real, observed output from that broker. Where a lesson describes behavior at a scale or in a configuration this single-broker lab couldn't reproduce (a true multi-datacenter outage, for instance), it says so plainly.

Prerequisites: basic command-line comfort and a general sense of client-server networking. No prior messaging-system experience assumed. You need Java 17 or newer to run the labs yourself.

docs.title: 01 · What Kafka Actually Is: The Log-Based Messaging Model
docs.text: If you've used a traditional message queue (RabbitMQ, SQS, ActiveMQ), the first thing that trips people up about Kafka is that it doesn't delete a message once someone reads it. That single difference — a message staying in place after delivery — is the clue to what Kafka actually is underneath the "messaging system" label: a distributed, append-only log, not a queue at all.

docs.title: A topic is a log, split into partitions
docs.text: A topic is a named stream of records. Internally, a topic is split into one or more partitions, and each partition is, physically, an append-only log file on disk: new records are always written at the end, records are never modified in place, and each record gets a sequential offset — its position in that specific partition's log, starting at 0 and counting up forever (or until the record ages out, Lesson 9). Order is only guaranteed within a single partition — Kafka makes no promise about the relative order of records in different partitions of the same topic, which is the single most common source of "why did my events arrive out of order" confusion for people used to a single FIFO queue.

docs.title: Worked example: a real cluster, a real topic, a real version check
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --version
4.4.0

$ bin/kafka-storage.sh random-uuid
DfcdfOpkTYe9c0fXQmCgxQ

$ bin/kafka-storage.sh format -t DfcdfOpkTYe9c0fXQmCgxQ -c config/server.properties --standalone
Formatting dynamic metadata voter directory /tmp/kraft-combined-logs with metadata.version 4.4-IV2.

$ bin/kafka-server-start.sh config/server.properties
...
[...] INFO Kafka version: 4.4.0 ...
[...] INFO Awaiting socket connections on 0.0.0.0:9092. (kafka.network.DataPlaneAcceptor)

$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --topic demo-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1
Created topic demo-topic.

$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic demo-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
Topic: demo-topic   TopicId: _BAk3JKEQbWTWteNuFOUYw PartitionCount: 3   ReplicationFactor: 1    Configs: min.insync.replicas=1,...
    Topic: demo-topic   Partition: 0    Leader: 1   Replicas: 1 Isr: 1
    Topic: demo-topic   Partition: 1    Leader: 1   Replicas: 1 Isr: 1
    Topic: demo-topic   Partition: 2    Leader: 1   Replicas: 1 Isr: 1

(Real output from this course's lab broker — Kafka 4.4.0, the current release at the time this course was written, running entirely without ZooKeeper.) kafka-storage.sh format is a one-time step that initializes this broker's on-disk metadata before it can start at all — notice it mentions metadata.version 4.4-IV2, a version for the cluster's internal metadata format, separate from the Kafka software version itself. --create with --partitions 3 splits demo-topic into three independent logs from the start, and --describe confirms each partition has its own leader (broker 1 for all three here, since this lab runs a single broker) and its own ISR (in-sync replica set, Lesson 7) — each partition is tracked and replicated completely independently of its siblings.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The append-only, immutable-once-written design is what makes several of Kafka's defining properties possible at once. Because records are never modified, multiple consumers can read the same partition at their own pace without any locking or coordination — a consumer reading offset 1,000 doesn't block, or get blocked by, another consumer reading offset 50,000 of the same partition; each just tracks its own position. Because a producer only ever appends, writes are sequential disk I/O (fast, even on spinning disks, because there's no seeking around to overwrite existing data) rather than random-access updates. And because nothing is deleted on read, a topic can serve both "give me only new messages from now on" and "replay everything from the beginning" use cases from the exact same data, which a traditional destroy-on-consume queue structurally cannot do — once a queue message is acknowledged and removed, a second consumer that wants to reprocess history has nothing left to read.

Partitioning is also the unit of parallelism and the unit of ordering at the same time, and that pairing is deliberate: Kafka could have offered strict ordering across an entire topic, but only by serializing all writes and reads through one partition, which would cap throughput at whatever a single disk and a single consumer thread could handle. Splitting into partitions lets multiple producers write and multiple consumers read in parallel — real horizontal scalability — at the cost of only guaranteeing order within each partition. This is why key-based partitioning (Lesson 4) matters so much in practice: if you need all events for one customer, one device, or one order to stay in order relative to each other, you need them routed to the same partition, not spread arbitrarily across all of them.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting global ordering across an entire topic. Kafka guarantees order within a partition only — if your application logic silently assumes topic-wide ordering, it will work fine with one partition and then mysteriously reorder itself the moment you scale to more.
  • Treating Kafka as "just a faster queue" and missing the replay capability. Because records aren't deleted on consumption, a new consumer group can read a topic from the very beginning at any time — a capability traditional queues don't offer, and a common reason teams reach for Kafka specifically for use cases needing replay, audit, or multiple independent consumers of the same event stream.
  • Assuming "the log" is one single physical file. As the --describe output above shows, it's one log per partition, each independently tracked, leader-assigned, and replicated — "the topic's log" is really a set of separate logs working together.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a topic with 4 partitions, then produce 20 messages to it without specifying a key (so they land on partitions essentially at random). Use kafka-console-consumer.sh --property print.partition=true to see which partition each message landed on, and count how evenly they spread. Then predict, before running it: if you instead produced all 20 messages with the same key, which partition would they all land on, and why — confirm your prediction with the same consumer command.

docs.title: 02 · Brokers, Clusters & KRaft
docs.text: For most of Kafka's history, every cluster needed a separate system — Apache ZooKeeper — just to track cluster metadata: which brokers exist, which partition leader is where, what the current topic configuration is. As of Kafka 4.0, ZooKeeper support was removed entirely. Every broker now participates in (or talks to) a KRaft metadata quorum built directly into Kafka itself. This lesson looks at both what a broker does and what that quorum actually looks like, running for real.

docs.title: What a broker actually does
docs.text: A broker is a single Kafka server process: it holds some set of partition logs on local disk, serves produce and fetch requests for the partitions it leads, and replicates data for partitions where it's a follower. A cluster is a set of brokers working together, each one typically leading some partitions and following others — there's no single, special "the server"; every write and read routes to whichever broker currently leads the relevant partition.

docs.title: Worked example: a real broker's role configuration and a real quorum status
docs.text:
$ cat config/server.properties | grep -E "process.roles|node.id|controller"
process.roles=broker,controller
node.id=1
controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers=localhost:9093
controller.listener.names=CONTROLLER

$ bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 describe --status
ClusterId:              DfcdfOpkTYe9c0fXQmCgxQ
LeaderId:               1
LeaderEpoch:            1
HighWatermark:          1065
MaxFollowerLag:         0
MaxFollowerLagTimeMs:   0
CurrentVoters:          [{"id": 1, "directoryId": "ddnwqk4sQTmMSOUxo0xWhg", "endpoints": ["CONTROLLER://localhost:9093"]}]
CurrentObservers:       []

(Real output from this course's lab broker.) process.roles=broker,controller is the key line: this single node is running both roles at once — a --standalone configuration suitable for development, where one process both serves client traffic (broker) and participates in the metadata quorum (controller). A real production cluster typically dedicates separate nodes to each role, or at least runs multiple controller nodes for fault tolerance, rather than combining both on one process as this lab does for simplicity. kafka-metadata-quorum.sh describe --status queries the controller quorum itself, not the broker's data — LeaderId: 1 names which controller node currently leads metadata decisions, CurrentVoters lists every node with a vote in that quorum (just one, here, since this is a single-node lab), and HighWatermark tracks how far the quorum's internal metadata log has been durably committed — genuinely the same leader/follower/log model from Lesson 1, just applied to Kafka's own metadata instead of application data.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
KRaft implements the Raft consensus algorithm directly inside Kafka to replicate cluster metadata (topic configs, partition assignments, ACLs, broker membership) across a small set of controller nodes, the same way application data is replicated across partition replicas. This is architecturally cleaner than the old ZooKeeper-based design for a simple reason: before KRaft, Kafka had two separate replication/consensus systems running side by side — ZooKeeper's own protocol for metadata, and Kafka's own leader/ISR model for partition data — which meant two systems to operate, upgrade, and reason about for failure scenarios. KRaft collapses this to one: metadata is just another Raft-replicated log, using the same mental model (leaders, followers, a high-water mark) this course already introduces for ordinary topic partitions in Lesson 1.

The practical consequence worth understanding is controller quorum size. A KRaft quorum needs a majority of its voters available to elect a leader and keep making progress — exactly like Raft in general, and exactly like why ZooKeeper deployments traditionally used an odd number of nodes (3 or 5). A single-voter quorum, as in this lab, has zero fault tolerance: if that one controller node goes down, the entire cluster's metadata plane is unavailable, even though this is perfectly fine for local development. A production cluster uses an odd number of controller nodes (commonly 3) specifically so the quorum can lose one node and still have a majority to keep electing a leader and committing metadata changes.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running a single-controller-voter KRaft setup in production "because it worked in development." As shown above, a one-voter quorum has no tolerance for that controller going down — always use an odd-numbered, multi-node controller quorum (typically 3) for anything beyond local testing.
  • Confusing the controller quorum's health with broker (data-plane) health. kafka-metadata-quorum.sh describe reports on the metadata quorum specifically; a broker can be serving produce/fetch traffic perfectly fine even while the controller quorum has its own, separate state to check — they're related but distinct failure domains.
  • Assuming "no ZooKeeper" means "no consensus system at all." KRaft didn't remove the need for distributed consensus over cluster metadata — it moved that consensus inside Kafka itself, using Raft instead of ZooKeeper's own protocol (ZAB). The operational need for an odd, fault-tolerant quorum size didn't go away.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server <host:port> describe --status against any Kafka 4.x cluster you have access to (or this lesson's own lab setup) and identify: the current leader's node ID, how many voters are in CurrentVoters, and whether that number is odd (as a healthy quorum size should be). If you only have a single-node lab like this lesson's, explain in your own words what would happen to the whole cluster if that one node's controller process crashed.

docs.title: 03 · Topics & Partitions: How the Log Is Really Stored
docs.text: Lesson 1 described a partition as "an append-only log file." This lesson looks at what that actually means on disk — not metaphorically, but by opening the real files a partition is made of and dumping their contents with Kafka's own tooling.

docs.title: What's really in a partition's directory
docs.text: Each partition lives in its own directory, named <topic>-<partition> (so demo-topic-0, demo-topic-1, demo-topic-2 for Lesson 1's three-partition topic). Inside, the log isn't one single ever-growing file — it's split into segments, each a trio of files sharing a base-offset filename: a .log file (the actual records), a .index file (an offset-to-byte-position index, so Kafka doesn't have to scan the whole log file to find a given offset), and a .timeindex file (a timestamp-to-offset index, used for time-based lookups like "give me everything after this timestamp").

docs.title: Worked example: a real partition directory and a real log dump
docs.text:
$ ls -la /tmp/kraft-combined-logs/demo-topic-0/
-rw-r--r--  10485760 00000000000000000000.index
-rw-r--r--       100 00000000000000000000.log
-rw-r--r--  10485756 00000000000000000000.timeindex
-rw-r--r--         8 leader-epoch-checkpoint
-rw-r--r--        43 partition.metadata

$ bin/kafka-dump-log.sh --files /tmp/kraft-combined-logs/demo-topic-0/00000000000000000000.log --print-data-log
Dumping /tmp/kraft-combined-logs/demo-topic-0/00000000000000000000.log
Log starting offset: 0
baseOffset: 0 lastOffset: 2 count: 3 baseSequence: 0 lastSequence: 2 producerId: 0 producerEpoch: 0
  partitionLeaderEpoch: 0 isTransactional: false isControl: false position: 0 CreateTime: 1792846095985
  size: 100 magic: 2 compresscodec: none crc: 3648714602 isvalid: true
| offset: 0 CreateTime: 1792846095977 keySize: -1 valueSize: 6 sequence: 0 headerKeys: [] payload: hello1
| offset: 1 CreateTime: 1792846095985 keySize: -1 valueSize: 6 sequence: 1 headerKeys: [] payload: hello2
| offset: 2 CreateTime: 1792846095985 keySize: -1 valueSize: 6 sequence: 2 headerKeys: [] payload: hello3

(Real output from this course's lab broker — these are the exact three messages produced in Lesson 1's worked example, read back directly from the raw file on disk, not through any Kafka client API.) The filename 00000000000000000000.log is the segment's base offset (zero, padded) — the offset of the first record it contains; a broker rolls over to a new segment file (named with the next base offset) once the current one hits a size or time limit (Lesson 9 covers this). The index files are large (over 10 MB each) despite this tiny segment holding only 3 records and 100 bytes — Kafka pre-allocates index file space up front (log.index.size.max.bytes) rather than growing it incrementally, trading some wasted disk space for avoiding repeated file-resize operations under load. kafka-dump-log.sh reads the segment's binary format directly and shows exactly what's really there: each record's own offset, creation timestamp, key/value sizes (keySize: -1 here means no key was set — Lesson 4 covers what changes when one is), and the raw payload bytes.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The reason Kafka indexes by byte position, not by scanning records one at a time, is pure performance: fetching a specific offset or a specific timestamp without an index would mean reading and deserializing every record from the start of the segment until the target is found — fine for a tiny demo segment, ruinous for a segment holding gigabytes. The .index file maps a sparse set of offsets to the exact byte position in the .log file where that offset's record begins, letting a fetch jump almost directly to the right spot and scan only a small amount from there. This is also why the dump above shows position: 0 for the batch starting at offset 0 — that's the literal byte offset within the .log file, the same number the .index file would store to let a future fetch skip straight there.

Records in modern Kafka are written in batches (the baseOffset/lastOffset/count line above describes one batch containing all three records, even though they were produced one at a time by the console producer tool) rather than one record per on-disk write. Batching is what makes Kafka's throughput possible at all: producers buffer multiple records client-side and send them as a single batch (Lesson 4 covers the exact configuration that controls this), and the broker writes and replicates that whole batch as one unit — far fewer, larger I/O operations than one-record-at-a-time would allow, at the cost of a small, tunable delay while records accumulate into a batch.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming more partitions always means more index/segment overhead that scales badly. Pre-allocated index files are per-segment, not per-record, so the fixed overhead is bounded and doesn't grow with how many messages a segment holds — the real cost of more partitions is elsewhere (more file handles, more replication traffic, more metadata), not index bloat.
  • Trying to read or edit .log files directly with a text editor "to see what's in them." They're a binary format with length-prefixed records and batch headers, not plain text — kafka-dump-log.sh exists specifically because the format isn't meant to be read any other way.
  • Confusing a partition's offset with a byte position in the file. They're related through the index but are not the same number — offset 2 is the third record logically, wherever it happens to physically sit in the .log file (position: 0 in this example because all three records landed in one batch starting at the very beginning of the segment).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Produce enough messages to one partition that you can find more than one segment file under its directory (you may need to lower log.segment.bytes significantly for a quick demo — log.segment.bytes=1024 creates new segments almost immediately). Run kafka-dump-log.sh --files <path> --print-data-log against each segment file you find, and confirm each one's baseOffset picks up exactly where the previous segment's lastOffset left off.

docs.title: 04 · Producers: Keys, Partitioning & Batching
docs.text: "Same key always goes to the same partition" is the rule everyone learns about Kafka producers, and it's true — but it's easy to over-extend into "different keys always go to different partitions," which is false, and this lesson shows a real, unplanned example of exactly that distinction happening on a real broker.

docs.title: The partitioning rule
docs.text: When a producer sends a record with a key, Kafka's default partitioner hashes that key and maps it to one of the topic's partitions — deterministically, so the same key always resolves to the same partition for a given partition count. When a record has no key, the default partitioner (since Kafka 2.4) uses sticky partitioning: it picks one partition and sends an entire batch's worth of unkeyed records there, then picks again (not necessarily a different one) for the next batch — spreading load across partitions over time without needing a key at all.

docs.title: Worked example: a real key-based partitioning run, including a real coincidence
docs.text:
$ printf "alice:order1\nbob:order2\nalice:order3\nbob:order4\nalice:order5\n" | \
    bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic demo-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --property "parse.key=true" --property "key.separator=:"

$ printf "carol:x1\ndave:x2\neve:x3\nfrank:x4\ngrace:x5\nheidi:x6\n" | \
    bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic demo-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --property "parse.key=true" --property "key.separator=:"

$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic demo-topic --from-beginning --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --property print.partition=true --property print.key=true --max-messages 14
Partition:2  carol    x1
Partition:2  eve      x3
Partition:1  dave     x2
Partition:1  frank    x4
Partition:1  heidi    x6
Partition:0  null     hello1
Partition:0  null     hello2
Partition:0  null     hello3
Partition:0  alice    order1
Partition:0  bob      order2
Partition:0  alice    order3
Partition:0  bob      order4
Partition:0  alice    order5
Partition:0  grace    x5

(Real output from this course's lab broker — nothing here was cherry-picked; this is exactly what came back.) Look closely: carol and eve both land on partition 2; dave, frank, and heidi all land on partition 1 — new keys spreading across partitions exactly as expected. But alice and bob — two different keys — both land on partition 0, every single time, alongside grace and the original unkeyed hello1/2/3 messages. This isn't a bug: alice's and bob's hash values happen to both map to partition 0 out of this topic's 3 partitions, purely by coincidence of the hash function and this specific partition count. The guarantee "same key, same partition" held perfectly (every alice record is on partition 0, every bob record is on partition 0) — but it never promised "different keys, different partitions," and this is a real, unstaged example of exactly that gap.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The default partitioner computes hash(key) % numPartitions (using the murmur2 hash algorithm specifically, not Java's built-in hashCode(), chosen for better distribution properties across typical key shapes). With only 3 partitions, there are only 3 possible outcomes, and with a handful of short string keys, two of them landing on the same bucket by chance is genuinely unsurprising probability — it would happen for some pair of keys more often than people's intuition expects (a version of the "birthday paradox": with few buckets, pairwise collisions are more common than they feel like they should be). This is exactly why key design matters for real workloads with skew concerns: if your actual key space happens to concentrate unevenly across hash buckets — very possible with a small number of distinct keys, as this lesson's handful of names demonstrates directly — you can end up with one "hot" partition carrying disproportionate traffic, and more partitions alone doesn't fix it if the keys themselves are the skewed part.

Batching is the other core producer mechanism: rather than sending each record in its own network request, the producer's client-side buffer accumulates records (per partition) and sends a batch once it reaches batch.size bytes or linger.ms milliseconds have passed, whichever comes first. This is a direct latency-vs- throughput dial: linger.ms=0 (the default) sends as soon as possible, minimizing per-record latency; a small positive linger.ms (even 5-10ms) lets more records accumulate per batch, which can dramatically increase throughput for high-volume producers at the cost of a small, bounded delay — Level 2's producer-configuration lesson measures this tradeoff directly rather than just stating it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming distinct keys guarantee distinct partitions. As this lesson's real output shows directly, that's not the contract — only "same key → same partition" is guaranteed; the reverse is a probabilistic outcome of the hash function, not a promise.
  • Choosing a key with very low cardinality (a boolean flag, a two-value status field) and expecting even load distribution. With few distinct key values, you're entirely at the mercy of how those specific values happen to hash — exactly the alice/bob situation above, but now unavoidable because there's no way to add more distinct keys to even things out.
  • Setting linger.ms to a large value without measuring the actual latency cost for your use case. Batching helps throughput, but every millisecond of linger is a millisecond every record in that batch waits before being sent at all — appropriate for a high-throughput log pipeline, likely wrong for a latency-sensitive request/response pattern riding on top of Kafka.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this lesson's exact key list (alice, bob, carol, dave, eve, frank, grace, heidi) against a topic with a different partition count (try 5 instead of 3) and see whether alice and bob still collide — predict first, based on the hash-bucket explanation above, then verify. Separately, pick 50 random short strings as keys, produce one record for each, and tally the partition distribution — compare it to what you'd expect from a uniform random assignment.

docs.title: 05 · Consumers & Consumer Groups
docs.text: A single consumer reading a topic is simple: it tracks its own offset and moves forward. A consumer group — multiple consumers sharing the work of reading a topic — is where the interesting mechanics live, and this lesson watches a real group grow from two consumers to three and back down to two, with real partition reassignment at every step.

docs.title: The core rule
docs.text: Every partition of a topic is assigned to at most one consumer within a given group at any time. This is the entire mechanism behind "consumers in a group never double-read a partition" — it isn't a coordination trick between consumers, it's a hard assignment the group coordinator (a role one broker plays for each group) computes and hands out. A consumer tracks its position per partition as a committed offset, stored in Kafka's own internal __consumer_offsets topic — so a consumer that restarts resumes from where it left off, rather than from the beginning or from "latest."

docs.title: Worked example: a real group, growing and shrinking
docs.text:
$ # two consumers join group "demo-group"
$ bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group demo-group --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
PARTITION  CONSUMER-ID
0          console-consumer-807b0133...
1          console-consumer-807b0133...
2          console-consumer-941413a0...

$ # a third consumer joins
$ bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group demo-group --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG  CONSUMER-ID
1          3               3               0    console-consumer-941413a0...
0          9               9               0    console-consumer-807b0133...
2          2               2               0    console-consumer-9d68c153...

$ # kill the consumer holding partition 1 (941413a0)
$ bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group demo-group --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG  CONSUMER-ID
0          9               9               0    console-consumer-807b0133...
1          3               3               0    console-consumer-807b0133...
2          2               2               0    console-consumer-9d68c153...

(Real output from this course's lab broker, three real console-consumer processes, started and killed in sequence.) With 2 consumers and 3 partitions: one consumer (807b0133) got two partitions, the other (941413a0) got one — an uneven but valid split, since 3 doesn't divide evenly by 2. The instant a third consumer joined, the group rebalanced to a clean one-partition-each split — notice 941413a0 moved from partition 2 to partition 1, a real reassignment, not just a new consumer picking up what was unclaimed. When that same consumer (941413a0) was killed, the group rebalanced again: partition 1 was picked back up by 807b0133 (the surviving consumer that already held partition 0), restoring the uneven 2-and-1 split from the start — and crucially, LAG stayed at 0 throughout, because the committed offset for each partition persisted in __consumer_offsets regardless of which specific consumer process is currently assigned to read from it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Offsets are committed to __consumer_offsets, a normal (if internal) Kafka topic, keyed by (group, topic, partition). This is why offset tracking survives individual consumer crashes and even entire group membership changes: the offset isn't "remembered" by any one consumer process in memory, it's durably stored in Kafka itself, and whichever consumer gets assigned a given partition next simply reads the last committed offset for that (group, topic, partition) key and resumes from there. This is also exactly why restarting a whole consumer group with the same group ID resumes where it left off, while using a new group ID (or --from-beginning on a brand-new group) starts over from scratch — the committed offsets are scoped to the group identity, not to the data itself.

The actual rebalance mechanics — how the coordinator decides which consumer gets which partitions, and whether every consumer has to stop reading while it happens — have changed significantly over Kafka's history, which is exactly what the next lesson covers in depth: the classic "stop-the-world" eager rebalance protocol, the cooperative incremental protocol that followed it, and KIP-848's newer consumer group protocol (the one this very lab's console consumer advertised as "production-ready" in its own startup banner).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming more consumers in a group always means more parallelism. A group can never usefully have more active consumers than the topic has partitions — any consumer beyond that count sits completely idle, since every partition is already claimed.
  • Confusing LAG with "the consumer is behind." LAG is the gap between a partition's LOG-END-OFFSET and the group's CURRENT-OFFSET for it — a healthy, keeping-up consumer shows LAG: 0 exactly like this lesson's example, and a consistently growing (not just momentarily nonzero) LAG is the real signal worth investigating (Level 2's consumer-lag project goes into this directly).
  • Using a brand new consumer group ID for a quick test and being surprised it reads from the very beginning or misses existing data depending on auto.offset.reset. A group ID with no prior committed offsets falls back to this setting (earliest or latest) — know which your tooling defaults to before concluding data is "missing."

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this lesson's 2-to-3-to-2 consumer sequence yourself against a 3-partition topic, running kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe after each change. Then try the opposite experiment: use a topic with 6 partitions and only 2 consumers, and confirm each consumer ends up with 3 partitions rather than one sitting idle.

docs.title: 06 · The New Consumer Rebalance Protocol (KIP-848) vs Classic
docs.text: Every console consumer started in this course so far has printed the same line on startup: "The consumer rebalance protocol (KIP-848) is production-ready!" This lesson actually tries it, and compares it directly against the classic protocol every earlier lesson has been using without naming it.

docs.title: Classic: eager, cooperative-sticky, and now a next generation
docs.text: Kafka's classic consumer group protocol works by having the group coordinator trigger a rebalance — recomputing the entire partition assignment — whenever membership changes (a consumer joins, leaves, or is considered dead). The original ("eager") version required every consumer in the group to stop consuming during a rebalance, even ones keeping their same partitions — a real "stop the world" cost on any membership change. Cooperative-sticky (a later, still-classic improvement) reduced this by only revoking partitions that actually need to move, letting unaffected consumers keep working through most rebalances. KIP-848 introduces a genuinely new protocol (not just a new assignment strategy within the old one): a different wire protocol between consumer and broker, with the broker-side group coordinator playing a larger, more active role in assignment.

docs.title: Worked example: a real classic group vs a real KIP-848 group
docs.text:
$ # classic protocol (the default — every earlier lesson used this)
$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic demo-topic --group classic-group --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
$ bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group classic-group --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --state
GROUP          COORDINATOR (ID)     ASSIGNMENT-STRATEGY  STATE    #MEMBERS
classic-group  localhost:9092 (1)   range                Stable   1

$ # new protocol, opted in explicitly
$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic demo-topic --group kip848-group --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --consumer-property group.protocol=consumer
$ bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group kip848-group --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --state
GROUP          COORDINATOR (ID)     ASSIGNMENT-STRATEGY  STATE    #MEMBERS
kip848-group   localhost:9092 (1)   uniform              Stable   1

$ bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group kip848-group --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
PARTITION  CONSUMER-ID
0          miNVqnueR7awZwRlkgbcNQ
1          miNVqnueR7awZwRlkgbcNQ
2          miNVqnueR7awZwRlkgbcNQ

(Real output from this course's lab broker.) The ASSIGNMENT-STRATEGY column is the clearest, most direct real evidence of the difference: range for the classic group (the classic default strategy), uniform for the KIP-848 group — a strategy name that doesn't even exist in the classic protocol. The consumer ID itself looks different too: classic groups generate IDs like console-consumer-<client-uuid> (visible in Lesson 5's output), while this KIP-848 group's member is identified by a short, coordinator-assigned token (miNVqnueR7awZwRlkgbcNQ) instead — a real, visible sign that the broker's group coordinator, not the client, is now the one assigning and tracking member identity.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The core architectural change in KIP-848 is where assignment decisions are made. In the classic protocol, one consumer in the group is elected the "group leader" and is responsible for computing the full partition assignment client-side, then distributing it to the other members through the coordinator — meaning assignment logic runs inside a consumer application process. In the new protocol, the broker-side group coordinator computes assignments directly, and consumers simply receive their assignment via a lighter-weight heartbeat- style protocol. This removes an entire class of problems where a slow, buggy, or incompatible client-side assignor could disrupt a whole group's rebalance — the assignment logic now lives in one place (the broker), versioned and tested as part of Kafka itself rather than as a pluggable client-side strategy every client library has to reimplement consistently.

The new protocol is also designed for incremental membership changes by default, in a stronger sense than cooperative-sticky: rather than recomputing from scratch and figuring out a minimal diff, the coordinator tracks assignments more surgically, aiming to disturb as few existing partition-consumer pairings as possible on any single membership change — the direct architectural descendant of the problem cooperative-sticky was already trying to solve within the limits of the older protocol's design.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming group.protocol=consumer is the default and forgetting to check. As shown above, it must be requested explicitly (per-consumer, via this configuration) even on a broker version that fully supports it — existing applications keep using the classic protocol until they opt in.
  • Mixing classic-protocol and KIP-848-protocol consumers in the same logical application and expecting them to form one group transparently. Treat a protocol switch as a deliberate, coordinated rollout decision across every consumer instance of a given group, not a per-instance toggle to flip casually.
  • Judging the new protocol's benefit only by watching --describe output on a quiet, single-consumer group (as this lesson's minimal example necessarily does). The real win — far fewer disrupted partitions during membership churn — only shows up under the kind of frequent join/leave activity Lesson 5's 2-to-3-to-2 scenario demonstrates; repeating that exact scenario with group.protocol=consumer is the natural next experiment.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Repeat Lesson 5's 2-to-3-to-2 consumer group experiment, but start every consumer with --consumer-property group.protocol=consumer. Compare the kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --state output (assignment strategy, member ID format) against Lesson 5's classic-protocol run, and note whether partition reassignment during the 3-to-2 shrink looks any different in how many partitions actually moved.

docs.title: 07 · Replication: Leaders, Followers & the ISR
docs.text: Everything in this course up to now ran on a single broker with replication factor 1 — fine for learning the log model, but it can't show the one property that makes Kafka trustworthy for real data: surviving a broker failure without losing anything that was already acknowledged. This lesson runs a real 3-broker cluster and actually kills one of them.

docs.title: Leaders, followers, and the in-sync replica set
docs.text: Each partition has exactly one leader broker, which handles all produce and fetch requests for it, and some number of followers, which continuously replicate the leader's log. The ISR (in-sync replica set) is the subset of replicas — leader included — that are fully caught up with the leader at any given moment. A message is only considered committed once it's been written to every replica in the ISR (governed by the producer's acks setting and the topic's min.insync.replicas, covered in depth in Level 2) — which is exactly what makes committed data survive the loss of any one broker in that ISR.

docs.title: Worked example: a real 3-broker cluster, a real kill, a real failover
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --topic repl-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --partitions 1 --replication-factor 3
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic repl-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
Topic: repl-topic  Partition: 0  Leader: 3  Replicas: 3,1,2  Isr: 3,1,2

$ echo -e "msg1\nmsg2\nmsg3" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic repl-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092

$ kill <broker-3-pid>          # the current leader, killed outright

$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic repl-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092,localhost:9094
Topic: repl-topic  Partition: 0  Leader: 1  Replicas: 3,1,2  Isr: 1,2

$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic repl-topic --from-beginning --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --max-messages 3
msg1
msg2
msg3

$ # restart broker 3
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic repl-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
Topic: repl-topic  Partition: 0  Leader: 1  Replicas: 3,1,2  Isr: 1,2,3

(Real output from this course's lab — a genuine 3-node KRaft cluster, a genuinely killed broker process, not a simulation.) Before the kill: broker 3 leads, and all three replicas (3,1,2) are in the ISR. After killing broker 3 outright: a new leader (broker 1) was elected automatically within seconds, and the Isr shrank to 1,2 — broker 3 dropped out because it's no longer reachable — while Replicas stayed 3,1,2, because the assigned replica set doesn't change just because one member is temporarily down; only the ISR, which tracks who's actually caught up right now, shrinks. Critically, all three messages produced before the kill were still readable afterward — nothing was lost, because they'd already been replicated to the surviving brokers before broker 3 went down. Restarting broker 3 brought it back into the ISR (1,2,3) as a follower, without taking back leadership — Kafka doesn't force leadership back to a recovering replica automatically by default.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Replication works by followers continuously fetching from the leader, the same way a consumer fetches — a follower is, mechanically, a special kind of consumer of its own leader's log. The leader tracks each follower's fetch progress, and a replica only stays in the ISR as long as it's fetching recently enough (governed by replica.lag.time.max.ms); fall behind that threshold, or stop responding entirely (as this lesson's killed broker did), and the leader drops it from the ISR, shrinking the set of replicas a commit has to reach before being acknowledged. This shrink is itself informative to monitor in production: a shrinking ISR under normal operation (not a deliberate kill) is one of the most common early signals of real trouble — a struggling disk, network partition, or overloaded broker falling behind on replication.

Leader election, when a leader fails, is itself coordinated through the KRaft controller quorum (Lesson 2) rather than through the data-plane brokers negotiating among themselves — the controller tracks replica state for every partition cluster-wide and picks a new leader from the remaining in-sync replicas the instant it detects the old leader is gone. This is exactly why replication and the controller quorum, though conceptually separate (Lesson 2), depend on each other in practice: data-plane failover speed and correctness rest on the controller quorum being healthy and responsive.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running replication factor 1 in anything beyond local development "to save resources." As this lesson demonstrates directly, a single-replica partition has zero tolerance for that one broker's loss — there's no ISR to fail over to at all.
  • Assuming a shrunk ISR self-heals as soon as the missing broker comes back. As shown above, the replica does rejoin the ISR, but not the leadership position it previously held — conflating "back in the ISR" with "back to its old role" misreads what actually happened.
  • Confusing Replicas with Isr when reading --describe output. Replicas is the assigned, intended set regardless of current health; Isr is who's actually caught up right now — a partition can show a full Replicas list while its Isr is dangerously shrunk, and that gap is exactly what's worth alerting on.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this lesson's 3-broker setup, create a replication-factor-3 topic, and produce some data. Kill the current leader broker and confirm via --describe that a new leader was elected and the ISR shrank. Confirm no data was lost by consuming from the beginning. Then restart the killed broker and watch the ISR heal — note which broker holds leadership afterward, and whether it matches your expectation.

docs.title: 08 · Delivery Semantics: At-Most-Once, At-Least-Once & Idempotence
docs.text: "Exactly once" is the phrase everyone wants and the hardest one to actually deliver honestly. This lesson builds up to it properly: what a producer can control on its own (at-most-once vs at-least-once), what idempotence adds on top of that, and real evidence — read straight from the log file — of the mechanism idempotence actually uses.

docs.title: Two honest options, and a third that needs more machinery
docs.text: At-most-once: a producer sends a record and doesn't retry on failure. If the write never reached the broker, the message is lost — but it's also impossible to accidentally send it twice. At-least-once: a producer retries on any ambiguous failure (a timeout, a dropped connection) until it gets confirmation. This guarantees the message eventually arrives, but a retry after a message did actually succeed (just didn't confirm fast enough) can produce a real duplicate. Plain retries alone can only give you one or the other — idempotence is the mechanism that lets a producer retry safely without duplicating, which is what lets you get both "never lost" and "never duplicated" together, at least within a single producer session.

docs.title: Worked example: real producer IDs and sequence numbers, read off disk
docs.text:
$ echo -e "msg1\nmsg2\nmsg3" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic repl-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092

$ bin/kafka-dump-log.sh --files /tmp/kafka-cluster/node1/data/repl-topic-0/00000000000000000000.log --print-data-log
baseOffset: 0 lastOffset: 2 count: 3 baseSequence: 0 lastSequence: 2 producerId: 1000 producerEpoch: 0 ...
| offset: 0 ... sequence: 0 ... payload: msg1
| offset: 1 ... sequence: 1 ... payload: msg2
| offset: 2 ... sequence: 2 ... payload: msg3

$ echo "msg4" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic repl-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
$ bin/kafka-dump-log.sh --files /tmp/kafka-cluster/node1/data/repl-topic-0/00000000000000000000.log --print-data-log
baseOffset: 0 ... producerId: 1000 producerEpoch: 0 ...   <- unchanged, first producer session
baseOffset: 3 lastOffset: 3 count: 1 baseSequence: 0 lastSequence: 0 producerId: 0 producerEpoch: 0 ...
| offset: 3 ... sequence: 0 ... payload: msg4

(Real output from this course's lab broker — nothing invented, these are exactly the fields the broker wrote.) Every record batch carries a producerId and a per-producer sequence number, starting at 0 for that producer and incrementing with every batch it sends. The console producer tool enables idempotence by default (it has been the client default since Kafka 3.0), which is exactly why this metadata exists at all even though nothing in the commands above asked for it explicitly. Notice the second producer invocation (msg4) got a different producerId (0 instead of 1000) and restarted its sequence at 0 — each new producer session (a new client process, in this case) is issued a fresh producer ID by the broker's transaction coordinator; the sequence numbering that enables duplicate detection is scoped to one producer ID's lifetime, not to the topic or partition as a whole.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
With idempotence enabled, the broker tracks the last sequence number successfully written for each (producerId, partition) pair. When a batch arrives, the broker checks whether its sequence number is exactly one more than the last one it accepted for that producer ID. If the producer retries a batch that did already succeed (the first acknowledgment was simply lost in transit), the retry arrives with the same sequence number the broker already has recorded — the broker recognizes this as a duplicate of an already-committed batch and returns success without writing it again. If a genuinely new batch arrives with the expected next sequence number, it's written normally. This is a purely broker-side, per-producer-session bookkeeping trick — no distributed coordination, no two-phase commit, just a running counter the broker checks — which is exactly why idempotence has very low overhead and is on by default.

Idempotence alone guarantees no duplicates from retries within one producer session, to one partition. It does not, by itself, give you atomicity across multiple partitions or multiple topics in one logical operation (writing to an "orders" topic and an "inventory" topic as one atomic unit, for instance) — that's what the transactional producer API adds on top (Level 2, Lesson 4), using a transaction coordinator and a two-phase-commit-style protocol to make a whole batch of writes across multiple partitions succeed or fail together, which is the actual mechanism behind Kafka's "exactly-once" marketing claim for multi-partition, multi-topic operations.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming idempotence protects against application-level duplicate sends, like a user double-clicking "submit" and your code genuinely calling producer.send() twice with different content. Idempotence deduplicates retries of the same underlying request at the client-library level; it has no idea two separate send() calls represent the same business event unless your own application logic makes them identical at that level.
  • Thinking "exactly once" means no possible duplicates anywhere in the pipeline. It specifically covers producer-to-broker delivery (with idempotence/transactions) and, separately, consumer processing when done correctly (reading and committing offsets transactionally alongside any output writes) — a consumer that reprocesses after a crash without transactional coordination can still observe or produce duplicates downstream.
  • Disabling idempotence "for performance" without measuring. The overhead is genuinely small (one sequence check per batch) and the correctness it buys is significant — turning it off is rarely the right lever for a real performance problem.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Produce a batch of messages with the console producer, dump the resulting log segment, and note the producerId and sequence values. Restart the console producer (ending that session) and produce more messages to the same topic — confirm you get a new producerId and that its sequence starts again at 0, exactly as this lesson's real run did.

docs.title: 09 · Retention & Compaction
docs.text: Kafka has two completely different answers to "when does old data go away," and picking the wrong one for a given topic is a common, costly mistake. This lesson runs a real compacted topic to the point where compaction actually happens, and dumps the resulting segment to see exactly what got removed.

docs.title: Deletion vs compaction: two different questions
docs.text: Time/size-based retention (cleanup.policy=delete, the default) answers "how long do I keep records around at all" — once a segment is older than retention.ms or the partition exceeds retention.bytes, whole old segments are deleted outright, key or no key. Log compaction (cleanup.policy=compact) answers a different question: "for each key, keep only its latest value, forever (or until a delete marker's own retention expires)." Compaction is what backs Kafka's own internal __consumer_offsets topic (Lesson 5) — you don't want the history of every offset commit ever made, you want the current offset for each (group, topic, partition), which is exactly a per-key "latest value" problem.

docs.title: Worked example: a real compaction, observed by dumping the log
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --topic compacted-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1 --config cleanup.policy=compact \
    --config segment.ms=100 --config min.cleanable.dirty.ratio=0.01

$ # produce 5 updates each for two keys: user1 and user2, versions 1 through 5
$ bin/kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic compacted-topic
compacted-topic:0:10

$ # wait for the log cleaner to run, then dump the closed segment
$ bin/kafka-dump-log.sh --files .../compacted-topic-0/00000000000000000000.log --print-data-log
baseOffset: 0 lastOffset: 1 count: 0 ...     <- version-1 batch: emptied by compaction
baseOffset: 2 lastOffset: 3 count: 0 ...     <- version-2 batch: emptied by compaction
baseOffset: 4 lastOffset: 5 count: 0 ...     <- version-3 batch: emptied by compaction
baseOffset: 6 lastOffset: 7 count: 2 ...     <- version-4 batch: KEPT (latest in this segment)
| offset: 6 ... key: user1 payload: version-4
| offset: 7 ... key: user2 payload: version-4

(Real output from this course's lab broker — 10 records genuinely produced, and this is genuinely what the log cleaner left behind.) The batches holding version-1, version-2, and version-3 for both keys now show count: 0 — the records themselves were physically removed from disk by the compactor; only an empty batch header remains at that position, a result of the compactor rewriting the segment with the superseded records stripped out. Only the batch holding version-4 survived, because at the moment compaction ran, version-4 was the latest value for each key within this now-closed segment. Notice version-5 (produced right after, into a new, still-active segment) doesn't appear in this dump at all — it's sitting in a separate, newer segment file that hadn't been compacted yet, because compaction only operates on closed segments, never the one currently being written to.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The log cleaner is a background thread (or pool of threads, log.cleaner.threads) that periodically scans for partitions whose "dirty ratio" (the fraction of the log that's newer than the last compaction point) exceeds min.cleanable.dirty.ratio, then rewrites eligible, non-active segments: for each key, it keeps only the record with the highest offset and discards the rest, producing new, smaller segment files. This is why compaction is sometimes misunderstood as instantaneous — it's not a rule enforced on every write, it's a periodic background rewrite, which is exactly why this lesson's example needed a short wait after producing before the compacted state became visible on disk.

Tombstones (a record with a null value for a given key) are compaction's way of expressing deletion: writing a null-valued record for a key, then letting compaction run, eventually removes all prior values for that key, including the tombstone itself, after delete.retention.ms passes — long enough that any consumer that was behind at the time of the delete still has a chance to see the tombstone and know the key was explicitly deleted, rather than the key's history simply vanishing with no explanation. Deleting too eagerly (a very short delete.retention.ms) risks a slow consumer missing the tombstone entirely and never learning a key was removed.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using cleanup.policy=compact for a topic that's really an event log, not a keyed "current state" store. Compaction actively throws away history — appropriate for __consumer_offsets-style latest-value data, actively wrong for an audit trail or event stream where every historical record matters.
  • Assuming compaction is immediate. As shown above, it's a periodic background process with its own trigger threshold (min.cleanable.dirty.ratio) — querying a compacted topic moments after writing duplicate keys can still show every version, which is correct, not a bug.
  • Forgetting that records without a key can't be meaningfully compacted. Compaction needs a key to know which records are "the same thing, newer version" — a compacted topic receiving null-keyed records has nothing to deduplicate against and will simply accumulate them.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this lesson's compacted-topic setup, produce several versions of two or three keys, wait, and dump the resulting segment yourself — confirm which batches show count: 0. Then produce a tombstone (a record with a key but no value — the console producer's --property null.marker=<DELETE> option can send one) for one of your keys, wait again, and check whether that key's prior values and the tombstone itself eventually disappear after delete.retention.ms.

docs.title: 10 · Project: A Producer/Consumer Pipeline with Partition Keys
docs.text: Every lesson in this level built one piece of the model: partitions are independent logs, keys decide which partition a record lands on, and ordering is only guaranteed within a partition. This project puts all three claims under real pressure at once: three genuinely concurrent, independent producer processes, writing interleaved events for three different keys, at the same time, to the same topic.

docs.title: The setup
docs.text:
kafka-topics.sh --create --topic orders --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --partitions 4 --replication-factor 1

Three "customers" — customerA, customerB, customerC — each have 5 sequential events. If this were a real application, these might be three different HTTP request handlers, each independently producing events for their own customer, with no coordination between them and no shared knowledge of what the others are doing at the same instant.

kafka-console-producer.sh --topic orders --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --property "parse.key=true" --property "key.separator=:" < prodA.txt &
kafka-console-producer.sh --topic orders --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --property "parse.key=true" --property "key.separator=:" < prodB.txt &
kafka-console-producer.sh --topic orders --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --property "parse.key=true" --property "key.separator=:" < prodC.txt &
wait

Three separate OS processes, launched at essentially the same moment, each independently calling the Kafka producer API with no awareness of the other two.

docs.title: What actually came out the other end
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic orders --from-beginning --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --property print.partition=true --property print.key=true --max-messages 15
Partition:0  customerB  event-1
Partition:0  customerB  event-2
Partition:0  customerB  event-3
Partition:0  customerB  event-4
Partition:0  customerB  event-5
Partition:2  customerA  event-1
Partition:2  customerA  event-2
Partition:2  customerA  event-3
Partition:2  customerA  event-4
Partition:2  customerA  event-5
Partition:3  customerC  event-1
Partition:3  customerC  event-2
Partition:3  customerC  event-3
Partition:3  customerC  event-4
Partition:3  customerC  event-5

(Real output from this course's lab broker — three genuinely independent, concurrently-running producer processes, not a simulation.) Every single prediction from this level holds up under real concurrency: each customer's key routed to exactly one partition — customerB to partition 0, customerA to partition 2, customerC to partition 3 — and within each partition, events 1 through 5 arrived in exact order, despite the three producers racing each other with zero coordination. No partition received a mix of customers (keys don't collide here, unlike Lesson 4's alice/bob coincidence — these three happened to spread cleanly across four partitions). This is the entire payoff of key-based partitioning stated as a provable fact instead of a claim: order-per-key survives real-world concurrent, uncoordinated producers, specifically because ordering is a per-partition property, and same-key records always serialize onto the same partition regardless of which process happens to send them or in what order those processes happen to be scheduled by the OS.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Nothing about this required locking, coordination, or awareness between the three producer processes. Each one independently computed hash(key) % numPartitions for its own events and sent them to whichever broker leads that resulting partition — the broker, not the producers, is what serializes the actual writes to each partition's log, by virtue of being the single leader every write for that partition routes through. This is the real mechanism behind Kafka's claim of "scalable with per-key ordering": you get genuine horizontal producer scalability (as many independent producer processes as you want, no shared lock between them) and strict per-key ordering, because the partition-routing step plus single-leader-per-partition writing is what does the serializing, not any cooperation between producers.

If this project's events had been produced without keys instead, the sticky default partitioner (Lesson 4) would have spread them across partitions by batch rather than by customer — meaning two events for the same customer, sent in two different batches, could easily land on different partitions with no ordering guarantee between them at all. The entire reason this project's output stays cleanly ordered per customer is the explicit key, not an accident of timing.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming this project's clean per-customer partition split is guaranteed rather than a hash outcome. As Lesson 4's alice/bob collision showed, different keys can land on the same partition by chance — this project's three customers happening to spread across three different partitions is a real result, not a structural promise the API makes.
  • Running concurrent producers without keys and expecting the same ordering guarantee. As explained above, unkeyed records use sticky, per-batch partitioning — two events for the same logical entity, sent in separate batches, have no guaranteed relative order without an explicit key tying them to one partition.
  • Treating "no coordination needed between producers" as "no partitioning logic happens at all." Each producer still independently computes the same deterministic hash(key) % numPartitions — the lack of coordination is possible because that computation is deterministic and identical everywhere, not because partitioning is skipped.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this project with a fourth customer whose key happens to hash to the same partition as one of the other three (try a few short names and check with kafka-console-consumer.sh --property print.partition=true until you find a collision, the way Lesson 4 found one for alice/bob). Confirm that even sharing a partition, each customer's own events still arrive in order — but that two different customers' events on that same shared partition can now interleave with each other in arrival order, which is expected and harmless as long as your application only needs ordering within a key, not across keys.

docs.title: Level 2 · Operating a Cluster
docs.text:
Level 1 showed Kafka working. Level 2 is about knowing why a specific configuration value matters, what a metric is actually telling you, and how to change a running cluster's shape without losing data. Every configuration change and every metric in this level was observed on a real local broker, not quoted from documentation alone.

What was run, and what wasn't

Producer/consumer configuration, exactly-once transactions, JMX metrics, log segment behavior, and partition reassignment were all exercised on this course's real single-broker lab. Multi-broker-specific behavior (reassignment actually moving data between distinct machines, quota enforcement across many tenants) is described from a single broker acting in all roles at once and says so; the mechanism shown is real even where the lab's one-broker scale can't fully reproduce a production cluster's scale.

Prerequisites: Level 1. Comfort reading JSON-ish configuration output helps for the metrics lesson.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Multi-Broker Clusters & the KRaft Quorum in Practice: what changes when you add brokers, and how the KRaft controller quorum tolerates failure.
  2. Producer Configuration That Actually Matters: acks, batch.size, linger.ms, compression.type, measured, not just defined.
  3. Consumer Configuration & Fetch Tuning: fetch.min.bytes, max.poll.records, session timeouts, and their real throughput/latency tradeoffs.
  4. Exactly-Once Semantics: the idempotent producer and the transactional API, run for real.
  5. Monitoring: The Metrics That Actually Matter: consumer lag, under-replicated partitions, request latency — read from a real JMX endpoint.
  6. Log Segments, Indexes & Cleanup in Practice: watching segments roll and old ones get deleted, on disk, in real time.
  7. Security: SASL, SSL & ACLs: authenticating and authorizing a real client against a real broker.
  8. Partition Reassignment & Scaling a Cluster: moving partitions without losing messages.
  9. Quotas & Multi-Tenancy: throttling one client without starving the rest.
  10. Project: Diagnose a Consumer Lag Problem: a real, deliberately slow consumer, found and explained with real tools.

docs.title: After Level 2
docs.text: Level 3 builds on top of the broker: Kafka Connect for moving data in and out without custom client code, and Kafka Streams for processing it as it arrives.

docs.title: 01 · Multi-Broker Clusters & the KRaft Quorum in Practice
docs.text: Level 1 introduced the KRaft controller quorum and stated that it needs a majority of voters to make progress. This lesson proves it two ways on a real 3-node cluster: once by losing a minority (and watching everything keep working), and once by losing a majority (and watching a real metadata operation genuinely hang).

docs.title: Worked example: losing one voter out of three — no problem
docs.text:
$ kill <node-1-pid>          # 1 of 3 controller voters down

$ bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9094 describe --status
LeaderId:        2
CurrentVoters:   [{"id": 1, ...}, {"id": 2, ...}, {"id": 3, ...}]

$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --topic quorum-test --bootstrap-server localhost:9094 \
    --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
Created topic quorum-test.

(Real output from this course's lab cluster.) With node 1 down, 2 of 3 voters are still reachable — still a majority. The quorum leader (node 2, unaffected since it wasn't the one killed) kept working, and a real metadata operation (creating a topic, which requires committing a change through the controller quorum) succeeded immediately, with no visible disruption at all.

docs.title: Worked example: losing a second voter — a real, genuine hang
docs.text:
$ kill <node-3-pid>          # now 2 of 3 controller voters down; only node 2 remains

$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --topic quorum-test2 --bootstrap-server localhost:9094 \
    --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
(hangs — no response after 8+ seconds)

(Real output — this command genuinely did not return.) With only 1 of 3 voters reachable, there is no majority left to commit anything through Raft consensus. The create request isn't rejected with a clean error — it simply has nowhere to make progress, because committing a change requires a majority of voters to acknowledge it, and that majority doesn't exist anymore. Restarting the two killed nodes restored the quorum to 3/3, and the pending request (which the client was still holding/retrying) completed once majority was available again — a real illustration that a well-behaved client can be patient through a quorum outage rather than failing outright, which is a double-edged property worth knowing about operationally: your tooling may look "stuck" rather than clearly "erroring," and that's expected, not a bug in the tool.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Raft-based consensus (which KRaft uses directly, Level 1 Lesson 2) requires every committed change to be acknowledged by a strict majority of voters before it's considered durable — this is what guarantees that even if some voters are later lost, the committed decision isn't silently reversed, because any future majority must necessarily overlap with the majority that committed it. With 3 voters, the majority is 2 — losing 1 still leaves a majority; losing 2 does not. This is precisely why KRaft (and Raft deployments generally) use odd numbers of voters: an even number doesn't buy you extra fault tolerance over the next-lower odd number (5 voters tolerates 2 failures, exactly like 5; but a 4-voter quorum still only tolerates 1 failure before losing majority, the same as a 3-voter quorum, while needlessly costing a 4th node's worth of resources and network overhead for no additional resilience).

This is also why the quorum describe command kept answering during the minority-loss case — reads of the current known state can often still be served by a quorum that's lost some members, as long as a leader with a view of the committed log is reachable; it's specifically committing new changes that strictly requires a live majority.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a hung metadata operation as "the cluster is broken" rather than checking quorum health first. As this lesson shows directly, a hang with no error is the expected signature of a lost controller majority — kafka-metadata-quorum.sh describe --status against any surviving broker is the first diagnostic step, not a broker restart.
  • Sizing a controller quorum at an even number "for extra safety." As explained above, an even-sized quorum doesn't improve fault tolerance over the next odd number down — it only adds cost and complexity.
  • Assuming killing a controller voter immediately breaks client-facing broker traffic. As this lesson's first test shows, losing a controller-quorum minority doesn't stop existing partitions from serving produce/fetch traffic at all — only new metadata changes (new topics, partition reassignments, ACL updates) are blocked once majority is lost, not already-established data-plane operations.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: On a 3-node cluster like this lesson's lab, kill one controller voter and confirm (via kafka-metadata-quorum.sh describe --status and a real topic creation) that the cluster still accepts metadata changes. Then kill a second voter and confirm a metadata operation genuinely hangs rather than failing with a clean error. Restart both nodes and confirm the cluster recovers and any pending operation completes.

docs.title: 02 · Producer Configuration That Actually Matters
docs.text: "acks=all is slow, use acks=0 or acks=1 for performance" is common advice, and this lesson's own real benchmark numbers show it's an oversimplification — the honest result is more interesting, and more useful, than the folk wisdom.

docs.title: The configs that actually move the needle
docs.text: acks controls how many replicas must confirm a write before the producer considers it successful: 0 (fire and forget — don't wait for any acknowledgment at all), 1 (wait for the partition leader only), all (wait for every replica currently in the ISR, Level 1 Lesson 7 — the only setting that can't lose already-acknowledged data to a leader failure). linger.ms and batch.size control batching (Level 1, Lesson 4) — how long to wait, and how much data to accumulate, before sending a batch rather than sending immediately.

docs.title: Worked example: three real producer-perf-test runs
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic perf-topic --num-records 100000 --record-size 100 --throughput -1 \
    --producer-props bootstrap.servers=localhost:9092 acks=0 linger.ms=0
100000 records sent, 303030 records/sec (28.90 MB/sec), 5.16 ms avg latency, 24 ms 95th

$ bin/kafka-producer-perf-test.sh ... acks=all linger.ms=0
100000 records sent, 186916 records/sec (17.83 MB/sec), 225.45 ms avg latency, 250 ms 95th

$ bin/kafka-producer-perf-test.sh ... acks=all linger.ms=20 batch.size=65536
100000 records sent, 330033 records/sec (31.47 MB/sec), 1.72 ms avg latency, 4 ms 95th

(Real benchmark numbers from this course's lab broker — a 3-partition topic, 100,000 records, 100 bytes each, sent as fast as the client allows, on ordinary laptop hardware; your own numbers will differ, but the relationship between the three runs is the real point.) acks=0 with no batching gets a respectable 303K records/sec. Switching to acks=all with the same no-batching settings drops throughput by nearly half (186K records/sec) and inflates average latency more than 40x (5ms → 225ms) — this is the result that matches the folk wisdom, and it's real. But the third run — acks=all, with linger.ms=20 and a larger batch.size — beats even the first run: 330K records/sec, and the lowest average latency of all three (1.72ms). The honest conclusion isn't "acks=all is slow" — it's "sending records one at a time, un-batched, is slow, and that cost dominates far more than the acks setting does once batching is actually working."

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Without batching, each record effectively pays its own full network round-trip cost, and with acks=all, that round-trip includes waiting for the full ISR to replicate — which is why the no-batching acks=all run shows such high latency: every single record, individually, pays that full replication wait. With batching enabled, many records share one round-trip: the producer accumulates records client-side for up to linger.ms milliseconds (or until batch.size bytes accumulate, whichever comes first), then sends the whole batch as one request, and the broker replicates and acknowledges the entire batch as one unit. The ISR round-trip cost is still there with acks=all — it's just now amortized across potentially thousands of records in one batch instead of paid once per record, which is exactly why the batched acks=all run's average latency per record came out lower than the un-batched acks=0 run's: fewer total round-trips, even though each round-trip itself does more work (a full ISR acknowledgment instead of none).

This also explains why linger.ms=20 — adding a 20-millisecond delay before sending — produced a faster result, not a slower one, despite intuition suggesting "waiting longer must be slower." The 20ms isn't wasted time; it's exactly the window that lets many records combine into one efficient batch instead of many small, round-trip-dominated ones. The real tradeoff linger.ms controls is: too small, and you under-batch and pay excess round-trip overhead (as the second run shows); too large for your actual traffic volume, and you add real, unnecessary delay for applications where each individual record's latency matters more than aggregate throughput. There's no universally correct value — it has to be tuned against your own traffic pattern and latency requirements, the same way this lesson measured it rather than assumed it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Defaulting to acks=0 or acks=1 for "performance" without testing whether batching alone would have solved the actual problem. As this lesson's numbers show, the durability you give up with weaker acks settings may not even be the performance lever you think it is once batching is configured well.
  • Setting linger.ms to a large value by copying a benchmark's "optimal" setting without validating it against your own traffic volume and latency budget. A 20ms linger made sense for this lesson's high-volume synthetic benchmark; it would be a poor choice for a producer sending one record every few seconds, where that 20ms is pure added latency with no batching benefit to offset it.
  • Benchmarking producer settings against a single-partition, single-broker topic and assuming the numbers generalize. Partition count, replication factor, and real network topology between brokers all affect these numbers meaningfully — treat any one benchmark (including this lesson's) as directional, not as a universal constant to copy into a different environment.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run kafka-producer-perf-test.sh yourself against a real (even single-broker) cluster with at least three different acks/linger.ms/batch.size combinations, and record the real throughput and latency numbers for each — do not guess. Then identify, from your own results, whether this lesson's specific finding (batched acks=all beating un-batched acks=0) holds on your hardware too, or whether your numbers tell a different story — and if they differ, consider what about your environment (disk speed, network, CPU) might explain it.

docs.title: 03 · Consumer Configuration & Fetch Tuning
docs.text: Producer tuning (Lesson 2) had one honest surprise. Consumer tuning has two, in this lesson's own real benchmark: rebalance overhead dwarfing the actual data transfer for a short-lived run, and a "wait for more data before responding" setting making throughput measurably worse rather than better.

docs.title: The configs that actually matter here
docs.text: fetch.min.bytes tells the broker not to respond to a fetch request until at least this many bytes are available (or fetch.max.wait.ms elapses, whichever comes first) — intended to reduce the number of small, inefficient fetch round-trips when data arrives slowly. max.poll.records caps how many records a single poll() call returns to the application, controlling how much work happens per poll loop iteration. Session and heartbeat timeouts control how quickly the group coordinator notices a consumer has actually died versus is just slow — too aggressive, and a momentarily slow consumer gets kicked out and rebalanced away unnecessarily; too lax, and a genuinely dead consumer's partitions sit unprocessed longer than necessary before reassignment.

docs.title: Worked example: two real consumer-perf-test runs
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-consumer-perf-test.sh --topic perf-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --messages 200000
start.time, end.time, data.consumed.in.MB, MB.sec, nMsg, nMsg.sec, rebalance.time.ms, fetch.time.ms, fetch.nMsg.sec
2026-10-24 18:44:59, 2026-10-24 18:45:02, 38.1470, 11.6550, 200000, 61106.0189, 3150, 123, 1626016.2602

$ bin/kafka-consumer-perf-test.sh --topic perf-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --messages 200000 \
    --command-property fetch.min.bytes=1048576 --command-property fetch.max.wait.ms=500
start.time, end.time, data.consumed.in.MB, MB.sec, nMsg, nMsg.sec, rebalance.time.ms, fetch.time.ms, fetch.nMsg.sec
2026-10-24 18:45:26, 2026-10-24 18:45:30, 38.1470, 10.0705, 200000, 52798.3105, 3159, 629, 317965.0238

(Real benchmark numbers from this course's lab broker, 200,000 records already sitting in the topic for both runs.) Look at the column breakdown in the first run: rebalance.time.ms is 3150 — over three seconds — while fetch.time.ms is only 123.
