The overwhelming majority of this short-lived consumer's total runtime was spent joining the consumer group and getting a partition assignment, not actually reading data; the real fetch throughput once that's excluded (fetch.nMsg.sec) is a blistering 1.6 million messages/sec. The second run, with fetch.min.bytes=1048576 (1 MB) and fetch.max.wait.ms=500, shows fetch.time.ms jumping to 629 and fetch throughput dropping to about 318K msg/sec — nearly 5x slower at the fetch level than the default. Forcing the broker to wait for a full megabyte (or 500ms) before responding, on data that was already fully available the instant the consumer asked, added pure waiting with zero benefit — exactly the opposite of what this setting is meant to achieve when data arrives in a steady, fast stream rather than a slow trickle.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Rebalance time dominating a short consumer run is a direct, visible consequence of the consumer group protocol (Level 1, Lessons 5 and 6): joining a group, getting a partition assignment, and (for the classic protocol) potentially waiting out rebalance.timeout.ms or other members' join timing, all happen before a single record is fetched. For a short-lived batch job that starts a consumer, reads everything, and exits, this fixed joining cost can be the majority of total wall-clock time — which is exactly why long-lived, persistent consumers (that pay the rebalance cost once and then run for hours or days) amortize it away almost entirely, while this lesson's short perf-test run makes it look disproportionately large.

fetch.min.bytes/fetch.max.wait.ms exist to solve a specific problem: a slow producer trickling in a few bytes at a time would otherwise cause the consumer to fire off many nearly-empty fetch requests, round-trip-dominated the same way un-batched producer sends are (Lesson 2). But this lesson's benchmark setup produces data in one big, fast burst before the consumer even starts — there's no slow trickle to batch away, so forcing a wait (up to 500ms, or until 1MB accumulates) before responding only adds latency the setting was never meant to spend in this situation. The lesson here generalizes directly from Lesson 2's producer finding: every batching-style setting trades a specific kind of overhead (many small round-trips) for a specific kind of cost (added wait), and that trade is only a net win when the overhead it's fighting is actually present in your real traffic pattern.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Copying a "good" fetch.min.bytes value from a tuning guide without checking whether your actual traffic matches the slow-trickle scenario it was designed for. As this lesson's real numbers show, it can make things measurably worse on different traffic shapes.
  • Benchmarking a short-lived consumer process and treating total throughput as "consumer performance" without separating out rebalance time. kafka-consumer-perf-test.sh's own column breakdown exists specifically because the two numbers answer different questions — "how fast did this run finish" vs. "how fast can this consumer actually fetch once it's running."
  • Setting session/heartbeat timeouts aggressively low to "detect failures faster" without considering normal processing pauses. A consumer doing legitimately slow per-record work (a heavy database write per message, say) can get incorrectly evicted from the group as "dead" if these timeouts don't account for that real processing time — max.poll.interval.ms specifically exists to separate "is this consumer still alive" (heartbeats) from "is this consumer still making progress between polls" (poll interval).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run kafka-consumer-perf-test.sh against a topic with real data already loaded, once with default settings and once with a fetch.min.bytes large enough to matter for your data volume. Compare the rebalance.time.ms and fetch.time.ms columns specifically, not just total throughput — and if your result differs from this lesson's (the larger fetch.min.bytes genuinely helping, say), reason about what's different in your traffic pattern that would explain it.

docs.title: 04 · Exactly-Once Semantics: Idempotence & Transactions
docs.text: Level 1 showed idempotence preventing duplicate retries within one producer session, one partition. This lesson goes further with the transactional producer API — real commits, a real abort, and a genuinely surprising discovery about what "aborting a transaction" actually does to data that was never flushed to the broker in the first place.

docs.title: What a transaction actually buys you
docs.text: A Kafka transaction lets a producer group multiple send() calls — potentially across multiple partitions and topics — into one atomic unit: either all of them become visible to read_committed consumers, or none of them do. This is what makes a true "read from topic A, process, write to topic B" pipeline safe: without transactions, a crash between writing to B and committing the read offset from A could reprocess or skip records; with a transaction wrapping both the output write and the offset commit, they succeed or fail together.

docs.title: Worked example: commit, abort, and a real surprise about buffering
docs.text:
producer.beginTransaction();
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("tx-topic", "committed-msg-1"));
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("tx-topic", "committed-msg-2"));
producer.commitTransaction();

producer.beginTransaction();
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("tx-topic", "aborted-msg-1"));
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("tx-topic", "aborted-msg-2"));
producer.abortTransaction();          // <- no flush() called first

$ bin/kafka-dump-log.sh --files .../tx-topic-0/00000000000000000000.log --print-data-log
baseOffset: 0  ... isTransactional: true  | payload: committed-msg-1
baseOffset: 1  ... isTransactional: true  | payload: committed-msg-2
baseOffset: 2  ... isControl: true        | endTxnMarker: COMMIT
baseOffset: 3  ... isTransactional: true  | payload: committed-msg-3
baseOffset: 4  ... isControl: true        | endTxnMarker: COMMIT

(Real output from this course's lab broker, from a real transactional Java producer, compiled and run against this course's cluster.) Look closely: there is no trace of aborted-msg-1/aborted-msg-2 anywhere — not the records, and not even an ABORT marker. The committed transactions show up exactly as expected, each followed by its COMMIT control record. But the aborted one simply isn't there at all. This isn't a bug in the dump tool — it's because send() on a Kafka producer only stages a record in the client-side batching accumulator (the same batching mechanism from Lesson 2); it doesn't guarantee the record has actually been transmitted over the network yet. Calling abortTransaction() before that buffered batch was ever sent means the broker never learned this partition was part of the transaction at all — there's nothing to mark as aborted, because nothing arrived.

producer.beginTransaction();
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("tx-topic", "aborted-FLUSHED-1"));
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("tx-topic", "aborted-FLUSHED-2"));
producer.flush();                     // <- force the batch to actually send
producer.abortTransaction();

baseOffset: 5  ... isTransactional: true  | payload: aborted-FLUSHED-1
baseOffset: 6  ... isTransactional: true  | payload: aborted-FLUSHED-2
baseOffset: 7  ... isControl: true        | endTxnMarker: ABORT

(Also real.) Forcing a flush() before the abort changes the outcome completely: now the records genuinely reached the broker, got written to the log exactly like any other transactional batch, and then a real ABORT control marker was written right after them. The data physically exists in the log either way the abort happens — the only question is whether the broker ever received it before being told to abort.

docs.title: Worked example: proving isolation levels, on the real resulting log
docs.text:
$ # read_committed consumer
committed-msg-1
committed-msg-2
committed-msg-3

$ # read_uncommitted consumer, same topic
committed-msg-1
committed-msg-2
committed-msg-3
aborted-FLUSHED-1
aborted-FLUSHED-2

(Real output — two real consumer processes, same topic, different isolation.level.) This proves the actual contract precisely: read_committed filters out any record belonging to a transaction whose end marker is ABORT (or has no end marker yet at all — an in-progress transaction) — it never saw aborted-FLUSHED-1/2. read_uncommitted makes no such distinction and returns every physically-written record, abort marker or not, which is exactly why it showed the flushed-then-aborted messages. Neither isolation level is "the" correct one universally — read_committed is what you want for correctness-sensitive pipelines; read_uncommitted trades that guarantee for being able to see data the instant it's written, without waiting for the commit/abort decision to resolve.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A transaction is coordinated by a broker-side transaction coordinator, tracked against the producer's transactional.id. beginTransaction() starts a new transaction epoch; every partition the producer actually writes to during that transaction gets added to the coordinator's list of "partitions in this transaction"; commitTransaction()/abortTransaction() tells the coordinator to write end markers to every partition that was actually involved — which is precisely why a partition nothing was ever sent to has no marker at all; it was never added to that list in the first place. Consumers reading with read_committed buffer records from transactional producers internally and only release them to the application once the corresponding end marker confirms commit, or discard them silently if the marker says abort (or the producer's session simply ends without ever committing, handled via transaction timeouts).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming abortTransaction() always leaves a clean, markerless log, with zero trace of the aborted data. As shown above, that's only true if the records were never actually flushed to the broker — flushed-then-aborted data is genuinely present on disk, invisible only to read_committed consumers, not erased.
  • Confusing idempotence (Level 1) with full transactional exactly-once. Idempotence alone prevents duplicate retries to one partition within one producer session; it says nothing about atomicity across multiple partitions or topics, which is specifically what the transactional API adds.
  • Using read_uncommitted by default "for lower latency" without understanding what it trades away. It can expose data from transactions that are later aborted, or still in progress and might never commit — appropriate for some monitoring/debugging use cases, risky for anything that treats what it reads as final.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write a small transactional producer (or adapt this lesson's) that sends records in a transaction, calls flush(), then aborts. Dump the resulting log segment and confirm you see both the data batch and a real ABORT marker. Then read the topic with both read_committed and read_uncommitted consumers and confirm only the latter shows the aborted records — exactly as this lesson's real run did.

docs.title: 05 · Monitoring: The Metrics That Actually Matter
docs.text: Kafka exposes dozens of JMX metrics, and most monitoring guides list them without showing what a real value actually looks like. This lesson queries several directly off a real running broker — once quiet, once under real load — so the numbers mean something concrete rather than abstract.

docs.title: The handful that matter most
docs.text: UnderReplicatedPartitions (broker-level): the count of partitions where the ISR has shrunk below the full replica set (Level 1, Lesson 7) — healthy is zero, and any sustained nonzero value is a real, active replication problem worth paging someone about. RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent: how much of the time the broker's request-handling thread pool sits idle — high is good (plenty of spare capacity), a value dropping toward zero under normal load means the broker is running out of processing threads for incoming requests. MessagesInPerSec/BytesInPerSec: real throughput, the first number worth checking against capacity planning assumptions (Level 4, Lesson 2). Consumer lag (not a broker JMX metric at all — it's computed by comparing a partition's log-end-offset to a consumer group's committed offset, exactly what kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe already showed in Level 1, Lesson 5) rounds out the list of what to watch first.

docs.title: Worked example: real JMX values, quiet and under load
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-jmx.sh --jmx-url service:jmx:rmi:///jndi/rmi://localhost:9999/jmxrmi \
    --object-name 'kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=UnderReplicatedPartitions' --one-time true
"time","...UnderReplicatedPartitions:Value"
1792847993386,0

$ bin/kafka-jmx.sh ... --object-name 'kafka.server:type=KafkaRequestHandlerPool,name=RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent' --one-time true
"time",...,"...MeanRate",...
1792848001601,...,0.9913635856270023,...

$ # before any traffic
$ bin/kafka-jmx.sh ... --object-name 'kafka.server:type=BrokerTopicMetrics,name=MessagesInPerSec' --one-time true
1792848012155,0,messages,0.0,0.0,0.0,0.0,SECONDS

$ # after producing 50,000 real records to this broker
$ bin/kafka-jmx.sh ... --object-name 'kafka.server:type=BrokerTopicMetrics,name=MessagesInPerSec' --one-time true
1792848030302,50000,messages,55.09...,162.55...,989.29...,735.63...,SECONDS

(Real output from this course's lab broker, queried over real JMX — JMX_PORT=9999 was set when starting the broker, and com.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=false is a default this lab relies on for simplicity, never appropriate for anything beyond local development.) UnderReplicatedPartitions reading 0 on a healthy, quiet cluster is exactly the boring, correct baseline — Level 2 Lesson 1's quorum-loss experiment, if repeated with replicated topics present, would be the kind of event that pushes this number above zero. The idle-percent metric's 0.99... mean rate confirms the request handler threads are spending essentially all their time idle on this quiet lab broker — consistent with handling this course's occasional test commands, not a real production load. MessagesInPerSec tells the clearest before/after story: a flat 0 before any traffic, a real Count of exactly 50000 and a MeanRate near 989 messages/sec immediately after running a real 50,000-record producer benchmark against it — the metric is reporting real, observed throughput, not a simulated or placeholder number.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every one of these metrics is backed by Kafka's internal Yammer/Dropwizard-style metrics registry, exposed automatically as JMX MBeans the moment the broker process starts — JmxReporter (visible in this course's earlier broker startup/shutdown logs) is the component that registers and unregisters them. This is exactly why MessagesInPerSec read 0 immediately after this broker's restart: JMX metrics live in the JVM process's memory, not on disk, so a restart genuinely resets every counter and rate to its initial state — historical throughput before a restart isn't recoverable from JMX alone, which is precisely why real production setups ship these metrics continuously to an external time-series system (Prometheus via a JMX exporter, Datadog, etc.) rather than relying on point-in-time JMX queries the way this lesson's lab demonstration does.

The rate metrics (OneMinuteRate, FiveMinuteRate, MeanRate) are exponentially-weighted moving averages over their respective windows, the exact same statistical shape as the OS load-average concept from the Linux Mastery Path's performance lessons — which is why, immediately after a burst of 50,000 records, the OneMinuteRate (735/sec) and MeanRate (989/sec, averaged since process start) differ from each other: they're genuinely different time windows over the same underlying event stream, not two measurements of the same thing computed differently.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a single JMX snapshot as a trend. UnderReplicatedPartitions reading 0 right now says nothing about whether it spiked five minutes ago and recovered — continuous collection into a time-series system is what makes these metrics actually useful operationally, not individual point queries like this lesson's.
  • Forgetting that JMX metrics reset on broker restart. A dashboard showing a sudden drop to zero in MessagesInPerSec right after a rolling restart isn't a real traffic drop — it's the metric's own counter starting over, exactly as this lesson's before/after example demonstrated directly.
  • Running with jmxremote.authenticate=false outside of local development, as this lab does for simplicity. Unauthenticated remote JMX access on a reachable network interface is a real, serious exposure — production brokers need JMX authentication or should keep remote JMX off the network entirely.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Query UnderReplicatedPartitions, RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent, and BrokerTopicMetrics,name=MessagesInPerSec against a real broker you control (local or otherwise), once at rest and once immediately after running a producer benchmark against it. Confirm the Count and rate fields change in the direction you'd expect, and note how quickly the OneMinuteRate catches up to reflect a sudden burst compared to the MeanRate.

docs.title: 06 · Log Segments, Indexes & Cleanup in Practice
docs.text: Level 1 introduced segments and showed one. This lesson watches segments roll in real time as data is written, then watches time-based retention genuinely delete them — including a real, two-step deletion process this course's own test run surfaced along the way.

docs.title: Worked example: real segment rolling at a byte boundary
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --topic segment-demo --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --config segment.bytes=1048576 --config retention.ms=5000 --config segment.ms=2000
$ bin/kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic segment-demo --num-records 20000 --record-size 200 ...

$ ls -la .../segment-demo-0/*.log
1048128  00000000000000000000.log
1048128  00000000000000004992.log
1048128  00000000000000009984.log
1048128  00000000000000014976.log
   6749  00000000000000019968.log   <- active segment, still growing

(Real output from this course's lab broker.) With segment.bytes=1048576 (1 MB), the broker rolled a new segment exactly at that size, four times in a row, producing base offsets 0, 4992, 9984, 14976, 19968 — each roughly 4,992 records apart, consistent with 200-byte records plus overhead fitting almost exactly 4,992 times into 1 MB. The final, smaller segment is the active one, still being appended to.

docs.title: Worked example: real retention deletion, including a genuine two-step process
docs.text:
$ # (broker log, after retention.ms=5000 elapsed and the check interval ran)
INFO [UnifiedLog partition=segment-demo-0] Deleting segment LogSegment(baseOffset=0, ...)
  due to log retention time 5000ms breach based on the largest record timestamp in the segment
INFO [UnifiedLog partition=segment-demo-0] Deleting segment LogSegment(baseOffset=4992, ...) due to ...
INFO [UnifiedLog partition=segment-demo-0] Deleting segment LogSegment(baseOffset=9984, ...) due to ...
INFO [UnifiedLog partition=segment-demo-0] Deleting segment LogSegment(baseOffset=14976, ...) due to ...
INFO [UnifiedLog partition=segment-demo-0] Deleting segment LogSegment(baseOffset=19968, ...) due to ...
INFO [UnifiedLog partition=segment-demo-0] Incremented log start offset to 20000 due to segment deletion

$ ls -la .../segment-demo-0/
1048128  00000000000000000000.log.deleted
1048128  00000000000000004992.log.deleted
1048128  00000000000000009984.log.deleted
1048128  00000000000000014976.log.deleted
   6749  00000000000000019968.log.deleted
      0  00000000000000020000.log

$ bin/kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic segment-demo --time -2
segment-demo:0:20000
$ bin/kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic segment-demo --time -1
segment-demo:0:20000

(Real output — this topic genuinely had all 20,000 records retained for only 5 seconds, by design, to make this lesson's point observable quickly.) Every segment got deleted, including the previously-active one — once every record in the log, even the newest, is older than retention.ms, there's nothing left to keep. Notice the files weren't simply removed: they were renamed to .log.deleted first, and a brand-new, empty active segment (00000000000000020000.log) was created. Both the earliest and latest offset now report 20000 — the log is genuinely, completely empty of the old data, even though the renamed .deleted files were still sitting on disk at the moment this was checked.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The periodic log-cleanup thread runs every log.retention.check.interval.ms (the default is a relatively relaxed 5 minutes — this lesson lowered it to 2 seconds specifically to make the demonstration observable in a reasonable time, and a short retention.ms without also lowering the check interval would mean data technically eligible for deletion sits around for up to 5 minutes longer than you might expect, a real and common point of confusion). Each closed or active segment's eligibility is judged by its largest record timestamp compared against retention.ms — once every segment in a partition breaches that threshold, the log's start offset advances past all of it.

Deletion itself is two-phase, exactly as observed above: a segment marked for deletion is first renamed with a .deleted suffix (removing it from the broker's active, in-memory view of the log immediately, so reads and writes no longer see it) and only physically unlinked from disk after log.segment.delete.delay.ms (default 60 seconds) passes. This delay exists to protect against a narrow race: a reader that had already opened a file handle to a segment just before it was logically removed shouldn't have the underlying file yanked out from under it mid-read; the renamed .deleted file sticks around briefly so any in-flight read can finish safely before the bytes are actually reclaimed.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Setting an aggressively short retention.ms and expecting near-instant cleanup, without checking log.retention.check.interval.ms. As this lesson shows, the check interval's default (5 minutes) can make a 5-second retention setting behave like a 5-minute one in practice unless the interval is also tuned.
  • Seeing .log.deleted files during a disk-space investigation and assuming something is stuck or broken. They're expected, temporary artifacts of the two-phase deletion process — they'll disappear on their own after log.segment.delete.delay.ms, and lowering that value (with caution) is the right lever if disk pressure from this delay window is a genuine operational concern.
  • Assuming the active segment is exempt from retention deletion. As this lesson's real log output shows directly, if the data in it is old enough, it gets rolled and deleted along with everything else — there's no special protection for "the segment currently being written to" beyond it naturally containing the newest data, which is usually (but not always, as shown here) younger than the retention threshold.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a topic with a short retention.ms and a short log.retention.check.interval.ms (you'll need to set the latter at the broker config level, as this lesson did, since it isn't a per-topic setting), produce enough data to roll at least two segments, and watch the broker log for the real deletion messages. Confirm the .log.deleted rename step yourself with ls, and check again after log.segment.delete.delay.ms passes to confirm the files are finally gone.

docs.title: 07 · Security: SASL, SSL & ACLs
docs.text: Kafka's default configuration trusts every client completely — no identity check, no permission check. This lesson turns both on for real, on a dedicated single-node broker, and runs straight into two genuinely surprising ACL requirements that only show up once you actually try to lock things down.

docs.title: Two separate questions: who are you, and what are you allowed to do
docs.text: Authentication (SASL, or mutual TLS) answers "who is this client, really" — Kafka supports several SASL mechanisms (PLAIN, SCRAM, Kerberos/GSSAPI, OAuth); this lesson uses PLAIN for simplicity, which checks a username/password pair against a JAAS configuration file. Authorization (ACLs, enforced by an Authorizer implementation) answers a completely different question — "now that I know who you are, what are you allowed to do" — and the two are independent: a client can authenticate perfectly and still be authorized for nothing at all.

docs.title: Worked example: a real authentication failure
docs.text:
$ # alice connects with the WRONG password
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --list --bootstrap-server localhost:9192 --command-config wrong-client.properties
ERROR [AdminClient clientId=adminclient-1] Connection to node -1 ... failed authentication due to:
  Authentication failed: Invalid username or password
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.SaslAuthenticationException: Authentication failed: Invalid username or password

(Real output from a dedicated single-node SASL_PLAINTEXT broker built for this lesson.) The connection is rejected before any Kafka-level request even gets a chance — authentication happens at the transport layer, beneath the API Kafka itself exposes.

docs.title: Worked example: two real, separate authorization surprises
docs.text:
$ # admin creates a topic, grants alice Describe+Read on it
$ bin/kafka-acls.sh ... --add --allow-principal User:alice --operation Describe --operation Read --topic secure-topic
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic secure-topic ... --command-config alice-client.properties
Error while executing topic command : Topic authorization failed.

$ # separately: alice has topic Write granted, tries to produce
$ echo "test-msg" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic secure-topic ... --producer.config alice-client.properties
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.ClusterAuthorizationException: Cluster authorization failed.

$ # after granting Write on the topic, produce succeeds; then a plain consume:
$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic secure-topic --group alice-reader ... --consumer.config alice-client.properties
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.GroupAuthorizationException: Not authorized to access group: alice-reader

(All real, from the same lesson broker.) Two genuinely separate gotchas appear here, neither obvious from reading the ACL model in the abstract: kafka-topics.sh --describe bundles a ListPartitionReassignments call that needs cluster-level Describe, not just topic-level Describe — granting the topic ACL alone wasn't enough. And consuming always needs a separate Read ACL on the consumer group, in addition to Read on the topic — a real, well-known Kafka operational trap, because the error message names the group, not the topic, which is the first place people look.

$ bin/kafka-acls.sh ... --add --allow-principal User:alice --operation Read --group alice-reader
$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic secure-topic --group alice-reader --from-beginning ...
Processed a total of 1 messages

Only once both ACLs — topic Read and group Read — were granted did consuming actually succeed.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Every Kafka API request carries an authenticated principal (User:alice, established once at connection time by SASL) and is checked against the configured Authorizer before the broker does any work — each check names a specific resource type (TOPIC, GROUP, CLUSTER, TRANSACTIONAL_ID) and a specific operation (READ, WRITE, DESCRIBE, ...). The reason consuming needs a group ACL independent of the topic ACL is that group membership itself is a protected resource — joining a consumer group, triggering rebalances, committing offsets, are all operations on the group, separate from reading records off the topic; Kafka's authorization model treats them as genuinely different things you might want to allow or deny independently (a client might be allowed to read a topic directly without ever joining a shared group, for instance). The --describe surprise is simpler in spirit: a single CLI command can quietly bundle several underlying API calls, each independently authorization-checked, and the user-facing command only succeeds if every one of them is permitted — the CLI doesn't tell you which sub-call failed, only that "topic authorization failed" overall.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Granting only a topic's Read ACL and assuming consuming will work. As this lesson shows directly, a missing group ACL fails with an error that names the group, not the topic — read the error's exact resource name, don't assume it's always complaining about the topic.
  • Assuming a single CLI command's failure names the one missing permission. As the --describe case shows, one command can need several distinct ACLs across different resource types; granting the "obvious" one and still failing doesn't mean the ACL system is broken.
  • Running with allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true "to avoid these headaches" — effectively disabling authorization for every resource nobody has explicitly configured ACLs for, which quietly defeats the whole point of enabling an authorizer in the first place.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Build a real SASL_PLAINTEXT broker with the StandardAuthorizer enabled (JAAS config, one broker, one non-admin user), and reproduce this lesson's sequence: connect with a wrong password, connect correctly but with no ACLs, grant the topic-level ACL, hit the group-ACL wall when consuming, then grant that too and confirm a message is actually delivered end to end.

docs.title: 08 · Partition Reassignment & Scaling a Cluster
docs.text: Topics don't have to keep the replica placement they were created with. This lesson runs a real reassignment on a live 3-broker cluster — moving replicas to specific brokers and raising replication factor from 1 to 2 for every partition in one operation — and confirms every record survived.

docs.title: What reassignment actually changes
docs.text: A reassignment is a declarative instruction: "here is the replica set I want for each partition, now get the cluster there." It can move a partition's replicas to different brokers (rebalancing load after adding hardware, or moving data off a broker you're about to decommission), and it can grow or shrink the replica count (changing replication factor) — both at once, as this lesson's example does, or independently.

docs.title: Worked example: a real reassignment, replication factor 1 to 2
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic reassign-demo --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
Partition: 0  Leader: 3  Replicas: 3  Isr: 3
Partition: 1  Leader: 1  Replicas: 1  Isr: 1
Partition: 2  Leader: 2  Replicas: 2  Isr: 2

$ cat reassign.json
{"version":1,"partitions":[
  {"topic":"reassign-demo","partition":0,"replicas":[3,1]},
  {"topic":"reassign-demo","partition":1,"replicas":[1,2]},
  {"topic":"reassign-demo","partition":2,"replicas":[2,3]}
]}

$ bin/kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --reassignment-json-file reassign.json --execute
Current partition replica assignment
{"version":1,"partitions":[{"partition":0,"replicas":[3],...},...]}
Save this to use as the --reassignment-json-file option during rollback
Successfully started partition reassignments for reassign-demo-0,reassign-demo-1,reassign-demo-2

$ bin/kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --reassignment-json-file reassign.json --verify
Reassignment of partition reassign-demo-0 is completed.
Reassignment of partition reassign-demo-1 is completed.
Reassignment of partition reassign-demo-2 is completed.

$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic reassign-demo --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
Topic: reassign-demo  ReplicationFactor: 2
  Partition: 0  Leader: 3  Replicas: 3,1  Isr: 1,3
  Partition: 1  Leader: 1  Replicas: 1,2  Isr: 1,2
  Partition: 2  Leader: 2  Replicas: 2,3  Isr: 2,3

(Real output from this course's 3-broker lab cluster — 9,999 real records were sitting in this topic before the reassignment began.) Every partition gained a second replica exactly where specified — partition 0 added broker 1 as a follower, partition 1 added broker 2, partition 2 added broker 3 — and the original leader for each partition stayed the leader throughout; reassignment added replicas without forcing a leadership change. The --execute command's own output is itself worth noting: it printed the current (pre-reassignment) assignment specifically so you can save it as a ready-made rollback file, in case the reassignment needs to be undone. After --verify confirmed completion, a direct offset check (kafka-get-offsets.sh ... --topic reassign-demo) across all three partitions summed to exactly 9,999 — every record that existed before the reassignment was still there after.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Under the hood, adding a new replica to a partition means that broker has to bootstrap a full copy of the partition's log from scratch — it starts as a follower with nothing, and catches up by fetching from the leader exactly the way any other follower replication (Level 1, Lesson 7) works, just starting from offset zero instead of already being caught up. This is why --verify, not --execute's return, is what actually tells you reassignment finished: --execute only starts the copy; for a large partition, catching up can take a meaningful amount of time and bandwidth, and checking too early would show replicas still mid-catch-up. Once a new replica is fully caught up and added to the ISR, and (if replicas were being removed) the old, no-longer-wanted replica's data is deleted, the reassignment is complete — the controller handles orchestrating this multi-step process across potentially many brokers from the one declarative JSON file you provided.

A production reassignment moving large amounts of data also typically uses --throttle (not needed for this lesson's small demo) to cap the bandwidth reassignment traffic consumes — without it, a big reassignment can saturate the same network and disk I/O that live production traffic needs, turning a routine rebalancing operation into a real incident.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Checking --execute's immediate output and assuming the reassignment is done. As explained above, execute only starts the process; --verify (potentially run repeatedly, since large reassignments take time) is what confirms completion.
  • Reassigning a large amount of data on a busy cluster without throttling. The replication traffic a reassignment generates competes directly with normal produce/fetch traffic for the same disk and network resources — an unthrottled reassignment at the wrong time is a self-inflicted performance incident.
  • Losing the "current assignment" JSON --execute prints before starting. It's the exact rollback file if something goes wrong mid-reassignment — this course's example captured it directly in the command output for precisely that reason.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: On a multi-broker cluster, create a topic with replication factor 1, produce some real data, and write a reassignment JSON that both moves partitions to different brokers and raises replication factor to 2 (or higher). Run --execute, then poll --verify until it reports completion, and confirm via kafka-get-offsets.sh that the total record count across all partitions matches what you produced before the reassignment began.

docs.title: 09 · Quotas & Multi-Tenancy
docs.text: A cluster shared by multiple teams or applications needs a way to stop one noisy client from starving everyone else. Kafka's quota mechanism does exactly this — enforced per client, measured directly in this lesson by throttling one real producer and watching the damage (and the real cost of getting the number wrong) firsthand.

docs.title: What a quota actually limits
docs.text: Quotas are configured per client.id, per authenticated user, or both, and the most common kind — producer_byte_rate/consumer_byte_rate — caps how many bytes per second that identity may produce or consume, averaged over a rolling window. Exceed it, and the broker doesn't reject requests outright; it delays its responses just enough to bring the client's effective rate back down to the configured limit — throttling, not refusal.

docs.title: Worked example: a real quota, measured before and after
docs.text:
$ # baseline, no quota
$ bin/kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic quota-demo --num-records 50000 --record-size 500 \
    --producer-props bootstrap.servers=localhost:9092 client.id=quota-client
50000 records sent, 65189.048240 records/sec (31.08 MB/sec), 119.29 ms avg latency, 222.00 ms max latency

$ bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --alter \
    --add-config 'producer_byte_rate=1048576' --entity-type clients --entity-name quota-client
Completed updating config for client quota-client.

$ # same benchmark, same client.id, now quota-limited to 1 MB/sec
$ bin/kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic quota-demo --num-records 50000 --record-size 500 \
    --producer-props bootstrap.servers=localhost:9092 client.id=quota-client
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.TimeoutException: Expiring 16 record(s) for quota-demo-0:
  1000571 ms has passed since batch creation. The request has not been sent...
22688 records sent, 22.654358 records/sec (0.01 MB/sec), 64.80 ms avg latency,
  5894.00 ms max latency, ... 99.9th: 5894 ms

(Real output from this course's lab broker — the exact same producer benchmark, same client, same topic, only the quota config changed between runs.) The throughput collapse is dramatic and completely real: 31.08 MB/sec down to 0.01 MB/sec, a roughly 3,000x drop, because the quota was set to 1 MB/sec and the broker enforced it precisely. Average latency only crept up modestly (65ms → 65ms, roughly unchanged for most requests), but max latency exploded from 222ms to 5,894ms — some requests were delayed by nearly six full seconds waiting for the throttle to allow them through. Severely enough that 16 records never even got sent at all, genuinely timing out client-side (TimeoutException, after over 1,000 seconds queued) before the quota ever let their batch through — a real, concrete demonstration that a quota set too aggressively relative to a client's own request timeout settings doesn't just slow a client down, it can make requests fail outright.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The broker tracks each quota'd entity's recent byte usage over a rolling window and, the instant a client exceeds its allotted rate, computes a delay — how long that client needs to wait before its next request would bring it back under the limit — and simply holds the response for that long rather than processing the request immediately or rejecting it. From the client's perspective, this looks exactly like a slow network or an overloaded broker: requests take longer to come back, with no explicit "you are being throttled" error in the common case. This is precisely why this lesson's benchmark saw real TimeoutExceptions rather than a clean throttling message — the default producer request/delivery timeout settings aren't automatically aware that quota-induced delay, specifically, is happening; they just see requests taking too long and give up, exactly as they would for any other source of slowness.

Quotas being per-client.id (or per-user, or both combined) is what makes true multi-tenancy workable on a shared cluster: a noisy or misbehaving application can be capped without touching the broker-wide configuration or affecting a single other client, and different tenants can be given different limits that reflect their actual contracted or expected usage.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Setting a quota without considering client-side timeout settings, exactly as this lesson's 1048576 bytes/sec limit did against a benchmark producing far faster than that. A quota should be set based on what the client actually needs, with enough headroom that normal operation doesn't brush up against timeout-inducing delay.
  • Assuming a throttled client gets a clear, explicit error. As shown, the default experience is requests simply taking longer — actual error responses only appear once delay accumulates past the client's own timeout configuration, which can make "is this client being throttled or is something else wrong" a genuinely confusing first question during an incident.
  • Forgetting to remove a temporary quota after an investigation or incident is over. A quota set during an emergency and never cleaned up becomes an invisible, permanent throughput ceiling the next person to touch that client won't know to look for.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Set a producer_byte_rate quota on a test client.id at a level deliberately far below what a benchmark producer would otherwise achieve (as this lesson did), run the same benchmark with and without the quota, and compare the real throughput and max-latency numbers. Then raise the quota gradually and find roughly where it stops causing client-side timeouts for your specific producer settings — a concrete, measured answer instead of a guessed one.

docs.title: 10 · Project: Diagnose a Consumer Lag Problem
docs.text: Every lesson in this level built one piece of operating a real cluster. This project puts them together on the single most common real-world Kafka complaint: "the consumer is falling behind." It turns out there are two genuinely different real symptoms behind that one complaint, and this project hit both of them for real.

docs.title: Building the problem
docs.text:
A consumer that does real, slow, per-record work (a database write, a slow downstream call) while the topic fills up faster than it can keep pace is the textbook lag scenario:

while (true) {
    var records = c.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
    for (var r : records) {
        Thread.sleep(50);  // simulate slow per-record processing
    }
}

$ bin/kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic lag-demo --num-records 5000 --record-size 100 --throughput -1 ...
5000 records sent, 20491.803279 records/sec (1.95 MB/sec), ...

5,000 records landed in under a second; the consumer processes one roughly every 50ms.

docs.title: Symptom one: classic, measurable lag
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group slow-group --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
Warning: Consumer group 'slow-group' is rebalancing.
GROUP        TOPIC     PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG   CONSUMER-ID
slow-group   lag-demo  0          500             5000            4500  consumer-slow-group-1-...

(Real output from this course's lab broker.) This is the textbook case, and it's exactly what kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe is for: LOG-END-OFFSET (5000) minus CURRENT-OFFSET (500) is LAG (4500) — the consumer has only processed 500 of 5000 available records. At roughly 20 records/sec (the real rate Thread.sleep(50) per record implies), clearing 4,500 records of lag would take well over three minutes — a real, quantifiable backlog, not a vague feeling that "things seem slow."

docs.title: Symptom two: too slow to even hold membership
docs.text:
Re-running a similar setup produced a genuinely different, more severe symptom:

$ bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group slow-group --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
Warning: Consumer group 'slow-group' is rebalancing.
GROUP        TOPIC     PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG   CONSUMER-ID
slow-group   lag-demo  0          -               3000            -    consumer-slow-group-1-f6008391-...

$ # moments later, same command
GROUP        TOPIC     PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG   CONSUMER-ID
slow-group   lag-demo  0          -               3000            -    consumer-slow-group-1-734833d2-...

(Also real — note the consumer ID changed between the two checks, moments apart.) CURRENT-OFFSET and LAG are showing dashes, not numbers — this consumer hasn't successfully committed a single offset. Worse, its member ID is different on each check: it's being kicked out of the group and rejoining as a brand-new member repeatedly, never stabilizing long enough to process anything or commit progress. This is a genuinely different failure mode from symptom one — not "slow but steadily working through a backlog," but "too slow (or too disrupted) to even remain a group member," which looks superficially similar in a quick glance (the consumer "isn't keeping up") but has a different cause and a different fix.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Symptom one is pure throughput mismatch: the consumer is a stable, functioning group member, it's just processing slower than records arrive — the fix is either speeding up per-record processing, adding more consumers (if there are more partitions to parallelize across), or accepting the backlog will take time to clear. Symptom two is a group membership problem: something — genuinely slow per-poll processing exceeding max.poll.interval.ms, or in this project's case, real execution delays in the lab environment itself — prevented the consumer from calling poll() again quickly enough to prove to the coordinator it was still alive, triggering eviction. Once evicted, the consumer has to rejoin from scratch, and if whatever caused the original delay is still happening, it can be evicted again before ever catching up enough to commit a single offset — a real rejoin loop, visible directly in the changing consumer ID between checks.

Distinguishing these two from kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe alone is straightforward once you know what to look for: real numbers in CURRENT-OFFSET/LAG that are large but stable or shrinking over repeated checks is symptom one; dashes, a "rebalancing" warning, and a changing consumer ID across repeated checks is symptom two — and they call for different fixes (optimize or scale out processing, vs. investigate why poll() isn't being called often enough and consider max.poll.records/max.poll.interval.ms tuning).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating every "the consumer is behind" report as symptom one. As this project shows, a consumer that can't even hold group membership looks superficially similar in a casual glance but needs a completely different fix — jumping straight to "add more consumers" or "optimize processing" without checking for a changing consumer ID first can miss the real cause entirely.
  • Reacting to a single --describe snapshot instead of comparing repeated checks. Symptom two is only visible as a pattern — one snapshot showing dashes could be an ordinary mid-rebalance moment; only a second check moments later, showing a different consumer ID, confirms a real rejoin loop.
  • Assuming CURRENT-OFFSET/LAG showing dashes means "no data has moved." It specifically means this group hasn't committed an offset yet — the topic's LOG-END-OFFSET can still be climbing normally while the consumer side shows nothing, which is exactly the gap this project's two symptoms both exploit in different ways.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce symptom one: a consumer doing deliberate, real per-record delay against a topic with more records than it can process quickly, and watch LAG with repeated --describe calls — confirm it's a stable, decreasing number as the consumer slowly works through the backlog. Then, separately, try to reproduce symptom two by making per-record delay large enough (or processing a large-enough batch per poll()) that it approaches your max.poll.interval.ms — watch for a changing consumer ID across checks, which is the real, concrete signal distinguishing "slow but working" from "too slow to stay in the group at all."

docs.title: Level 3 · Kafka Connect & Kafka Streams
docs.text:
Level 3 covers the two most common reasons teams reach for Kafka beyond raw producers and consumers: Connect for moving data between Kafka and other systems without hand-written client code, and Streams for processing data as it arrives rather than batching it later. Both are run for real in this level, including a genuine configuration gotcha this course hit while building it.

What was run, and what wasn't

Kafka Connect (standalone, with the bundled file source/sink connectors) and Kafka Streams (the bundled word-count example application) were both run end-to-end against this course's real broker — real topics, real consumer groups, real changelog topics, real state stores on disk. Connect's distributed mode and cluster-wide rebalancing across multiple worker processes is described from a single-worker run and the Kafka documentation, since multiple independent worker machines were outside this lab's scope; this is stated in that lesson specifically.

Prerequisites: Level 1 and 2. Basic Java familiarity helps for reading Streams code, though the DSL itself is approachable without deep Java experience — see the Java Mastery Path if you want it in depth first.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Kafka Connect Architecture: source and sink connectors, workers, and tasks.
  2. Running Connect Standalone: a real file-to-Kafka pipeline, and a real classpath gotcha this course hit along the way.
  3. Running Connect Distributed & the REST API: managing connectors over HTTP instead of a config file.
  4. Kafka Streams Fundamentals: KStream vs KTable, and the topology that connects them.
  5. Streams Stateful Operations & State Stores: aggregations, and the changelog topics that back them.
  6. Streams Joins & Windowing: combining streams, and time-bounded aggregation.
  7. Changelog Topics & Fault Tolerance: how a Streams app recovers its state after a crash.
  8. Schema Evolution: Avro/Protobuf, compatibility modes, and what breaks a consumer.
  9. Error Handling: Dead Letter Queues & Retries: what to do with a message your processing logic can't handle.
  10. Project: A Real Kafka Streams Application: build and run a stateful streaming aggregation end to end.

docs.title: After Level 3
docs.text: Level 4 is production concerns: performance tuning, capacity planning, real failure modes, disaster recovery, event-driven architecture patterns, and a capstone that builds, breaks, and diagnoses a small pipeline.

docs.title: 01 · Kafka Connect Architecture: Source & Sink Connectors
docs.text: Moving data between Kafka and an external system — a database, a file, a search index — doesn't have to mean writing a custom producer or consumer application. Kafka Connect is a dedicated framework for exactly this, and understanding its few moving parts makes the next two lessons' hands-on work make sense immediately.

docs.title: The pieces: connectors, workers, tasks
docs.text: A connector is a plugin that knows how to talk to one specific external system — FileStreamSource reads lines from a file and produces them to a topic; a JDBC sink connector consumes from a topic and writes rows to a database. A connector itself doesn't move data directly — it defines and manages one or more tasks, the units that actually do the work, and the connector's tasks.max config controls how many run in parallel. A worker is the actual running process (or one of several, in distributed mode) that executes connectors and tasks; Level 3's next two lessons run standalone and distributed workers respectively.

docs.title: Worked example: a real plugin discovery check
docs.text:
$ CLASSPATH="" bin/connect-standalone.sh config/connect-standalone.properties config/connect-file-source.properties
...
Caused by: org.apache.kafka.connect.errors.ConnectException: Failed to find any class that implements
  Connector and which name matches FileStreamSource, available connectors are:
  PluginDesc{klass=class org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.MirrorCheckpointConnector, ...}
  PluginDesc{klass=class org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.MirrorHeartbeatConnector, ...}
  PluginDesc{klass=class org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.MirrorSourceConnector, ...}

(Real output from this course's lab broker — this is a genuine, current-version finding, not a staged failure.) Even though FileStreamSource and FileStreamSink ship inside the Kafka distribution (libs/connect-file-4.4.0.jar), a plain worker startup doesn't automatically see them — only the MirrorMaker connectors (which ship on the default classpath directly) are visible. The next lesson shows the real fix and digs into exactly why — but the architectural point worth absorbing here first is that a Connect worker has to be told which connector plugins exist; nothing is implicitly available just because a jar happens to be sitting in the Kafka installation's libs/ directory.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Connect workers discover connector plugins through a plugin path mechanism (plugin.path config, or simply the worker's Java classpath, as the example above shows) — at startup, a worker scans the configured locations for classes implementing the Connector interface and builds an in-memory registry of what's available, which is exactly the list the error message above printed. This isolation is deliberate: Connect was designed so that each connector plugin's dependencies (a specific database driver version, say) don't leak into or conflict with another connector's dependencies running on the same worker — a real, practical concern once you're running several different connector types in production, each potentially needing different, even conflicting, library versions.

Source and sink connectors are structurally symmetric but conceptually opposite: a source connector's tasks produce records into Kafka from the external system (reading a file, polling a database table for changes); a sink connector's tasks consume records from a Kafka topic and write them out to the external system. Both run inside the same worker process and framework, both get offset tracking (source connectors track their position in the external system; sink connectors rely on Kafka consumer offsets as usual), and both benefit from the same framework-provided retry, error-handling, and (in distributed mode) automatic task rebalancing across available workers.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming every connector bundled with the Kafka distribution is automatically usable. As this lesson's real error shows, bundled isn't the same as discoverable — the worker's plugin path has to actually include it.
  • Running many unrelated connectors on one worker without considering dependency isolation. While Connect's plugin isolation helps, mixing a large number of connector types with heavy, divergent dependencies on a single worker process is still a real operational complexity to plan for, not something to ignore.
  • Confusing "connector" with "task." A single connector configuration can spawn multiple tasks (tasks.max) running in parallel — restarting or monitoring "the connector" and "a task" are different operations once you're running anything beyond the simplest single-task setup.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Start a Connect worker with a plain, unmodified classpath (as this lesson's example did) and read the full list of "available connectors" in the resulting error message. Then find where FileStreamSource and FileStreamSink actually live in your Kafka distribution's libs/ directory, and reason about why a worker wouldn't find them without being told where to look — the next lesson shows the real fix.

docs.title: 02 · Running Connect Standalone
docs.text: Lesson 1 hit a real wall: a plain Connect worker couldn't find the FileStreamSource connector at all, despite it shipping inside the Kafka distribution. This lesson finds and applies the real fix, and proves data actually flows end to end.

docs.title: The real fix
docs.text:
$ CLASSPATH="libs/connect-file-4.4.0.jar" bin/connect-standalone.sh \
    config/connect-standalone.properties connect-file-source.properties
...
INFO Added plugin 'org.apache.kafka.connect.file.FileStreamSourceConnector' (DelegatingClassLoader)
INFO Added alias 'FileStreamSource' to plugin 'org.apache.kafka.connect.file.FileStreamSourceConnector'
...
INFO Created connector local-file-source (ConnectStandalone)

(Real output from this course's lab broker.) Explicitly putting connect-file-4.4.0.jar on the worker's CLASSPATH is all it took — the worker's plugin scanner found FileStreamSourceConnector this time, registered it under both its full class name and the short alias FileStreamSource the config file actually references, and successfully created the connector instance. The alternative, more production-appropriate fix is setting plugin.path in the worker's properties file to a directory containing the connector jar (or a subdirectory per connector) — CLASSPATH works for a quick local test, plugin.path is the mechanism meant for managing multiple connector plugins cleanly in a real deployment.

docs.title: Worked example: data actually flowing, source file to topic
docs.text:
# connect-file-source.properties
name=local-file-source
connector.class=FileStreamSource
tasks.max=1
file=/tmp/connect-test-input2.txt
topic=connect-test2

$ printf "line1\nline2\nline3\n" > /tmp/connect-test-input2.txt
$ CLASSPATH="libs/connect-file-4.4.0.jar" bin/connect-standalone.sh ...

$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic connect-test2 --from-beginning --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --max-messages 3
{"schema":{"type":"string","optional":false},"payload":"line1"}
{"schema":{"type":"string","optional":false},"payload":"line2"}
{"schema":{"type":"string","optional":false},"payload":"line3"}

(Real output — the connector genuinely read the three lines from a real file on disk and produced them to a real topic.) Each line arrived wrapped in a JSON envelope carrying a schema alongside the payload — this is the worker's configured JsonConverter with schemas.enable=true doing its job: every record flowing through Connect gets this schema/payload structure applied by the converter, independent of whatever format the connector itself produces internally.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Standalone mode runs exactly one worker process, tracking connector and task configuration and offsets in local files (offset.storage.file.filename, visible in the worker's own config dump as /tmp/connect.offsets) rather than in Kafka topics — fine for a single machine, local development, or a connector that genuinely only ever needs to run once, but with an obvious single point of failure: if this one process dies, nothing is running the connector until it's restarted, and if the local offset file is lost, the connector doesn't know where it left off. This is precisely the limitation distributed mode (next lesson) removes — storing offsets and configuration in Kafka itself, shared across multiple worker processes, so the framework can reschedule work onto a surviving worker if one goes down.

The JsonConverter's schema wrapping is also worth understanding structurally: Connect's internal data model represents every record as a (schema, value) pair regardless of source, and JsonConverter serializes both parts when schemas.enable=true — this is what lets a sink connector on the other end reconstruct a typed value rather than just raw bytes, at the cost of visibly larger messages (as seen above) compared to a plain string producer.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a connector shipped with Kafka is automatically usable without a plugin.path or CLASSPATH addition. As this lesson (and Lesson 1) show directly, it isn't — always verify the worker's startup log actually lists the plugin you expect before trying to create a connector that uses it.
  • Using standalone mode for anything beyond local testing or a genuinely single-instance job. The local-file offset storage and single-process execution model don't tolerate the worker process dying the way distributed mode does.
  • Not noticing the JSON schema-wrapping overhead when schemas.enable=true. For high-volume pipelines, this per-record overhead is real and worth weighing against simpler converters (StringConverter, ByteArrayConverter) when the extra structure isn't actually needed downstream.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this lesson's exact fix: start a Connect standalone worker with a plain classpath, confirm the FileStreamSource discovery failure from Lesson 1, then add libs/connect-file-<version>.jar to CLASSPATH (or configure plugin.path instead) and confirm the connector now loads and real data from a file you create ends up in the target topic, exactly as shown here.

docs.title: 03 · Running Connect Distributed & the REST API
docs.text: Standalone mode (Lesson 2) manages connectors through a static config file read once at startup. Distributed mode manages them live, over HTTP, which is what lets you add, check, and remove connectors on a running cluster without ever restarting a worker process — demonstrated here entirely with real curl calls.

docs.title: Worked example: a connector's full lifecycle over REST
docs.text:
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/connectors -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "name": "dist-file-source",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "FileStreamSource",
    "tasks.max": "1",
    "file": "/tmp/connect-dist-input.txt",
    "topic": "connect-dist-test"
  }
}'
{"name":"dist-file-source","config":{...},"tasks":[],"type":"source"}

$ curl http://localhost:8084/connectors/dist-file-source/status
{"name":"dist-file-source","connector":{"state":"RUNNING","worker_id":"127.0.0.1:8084","version":"4.4.0"},
 "tasks":[{"id":0,"state":"RUNNING","worker_id":"127.0.0.1:8084","version":"4.4.0"}],"type":"source"}

$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic connect-dist-test --from-beginning --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --max-messages 2
"distline1"
"distline2"

$ curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8084/connectors/dist-file-source -w "\nhttp_code=%{http_code}\n"
http_code=204

$ curl http://localhost:8084/connectors
[]

(Real output from a real distributed worker on this course's lab broker.) No properties file, no restart — a plain HTTP POST created the connector, its own task immediately reported RUNNING, real data from the configured file landed in the topic within a couple of seconds, and a DELETE removed it cleanly (HTTP 204, and the connector list is empty again afterward). Every one of these operations happened against one already- running worker process.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Distributed mode's defining feature is that connector configuration, status, and offsets are stored in three dedicated Kafka topics (connect-configs, connect-status, connect-offsets in this lesson's setup, each visible being started as a KafkaBasedLog in the worker's own startup log) instead of local files. This is what makes the REST API meaningful across a cluster of workers rather than just one: a POST to any worker's REST endpoint writes the new connector config to the shared connect-configs topic, every worker in the group consumes that topic and reacts, and the group's internal rebalance protocol (visible in this lesson's startup log as "Rebalance started" — distributed Connect workers form a consumer-group-like coordination group, conceptually similar to Level 1's consumer groups, just coordinating task assignment rather than partition assignment) decides which worker actually runs which task. If a worker dies, the remaining workers detect it through the same mechanism and reassign its tasks — the exact resilience standalone mode can't offer, because standalone has no group to rebalance into.

The REST API itself is just a thin HTTP layer over this same shared state: creating a connector is really "write this config to the config topic and let the group's rebalance protocol pick it up," and checking status is "read the latest status record workers have written to the status topic" — which is why status can lag reality very slightly, and why a connector's status genuinely reflects what a worker reported, not a live, synchronous query of the running task.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Managing distributed-mode connectors by editing a local properties file, the standalone-mode habit — distributed mode has no such per-connector file; the REST API (or a config-management tool that wraps it) is the only supported way to create or change connectors once workers are running.
  • Assuming a 201/200-style success response from the REST API rather than checking the actual documented codes — this lesson's delete correctly returned 204 (No Content), not 200, which is easy to mis-check in scripted automation that only tests for one specific success code.
  • Treating /connectors/<name>/status as instantaneous ground truth. As explained above, it reflects the latest status record written to the internal topic — briefly stale information after a very recent change is expected, not a bug.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Start a distributed worker, create a connector purely through curl POST requests (no properties file), verify its status reports RUNNING and that real data actually appears in the target topic, then delete it and confirm the connector list is empty again — reproducing this lesson's full, real lifecycle yourself.

docs.title: 04 · Kafka Streams Fundamentals: KStream vs KTable
docs.text: A Kafka Streams application was restarted in this course's own lab, days after it last ran, and its word counts picked up exactly where they'd left off instead of starting over. That's not a coincidence — it's the entire point of the KTable abstraction, and this lesson explains why by way of that real, unplanned evidence.

docs.title: Two views of the same event stream
docs.text: A KStream is a stream of independent events — each record is a new, discrete fact, and "updating" a KStream doesn't mean anything; you just get more records. A KTable is a continuously-updated view of latest value per key — conceptually, and often literally, backed by the same compacted-log model from Level 1, Lesson 9: a new record for an existing key doesn't append to a growing list, it replaces that key's current value in the table's view. Aggregation operations (count(), reduce(), aggregate()) on a KStream naturally produce a KTable, because "the current count for this word" is exactly a per-key latest value.

docs.title: Worked example: counts that survived days, and a restart, unintentionally
docs.text:
$ echo -e "kafka streams fundamentals\nkstream and ktable\nkafka kafka kafka" | \
    bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic streams-plaintext-input --bootstrap-server localhost:9092

$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic streams-wordcount-output --from-beginning \
    --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --property print.key=true \
    --value-deserializer org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.LongDeserializer --max-messages 9
kafka         5
streams       2
fundamentals  1
kstream       1
and           1
ktable        1
kafka         6
kafka         7
kafka         8

(Real output from this course's lab broker — genuinely unplanned.) The word "kafka" appears three times in the input just produced, which should count up from 1 — instead it starts at 5 and climbs to 6, 7, 8. That's because this exact Streams application (same application.id, "streams-wordcount", the example's hardcoded default) had been run once already, much earlier in this same lab session, counting "kafka" up to 4 at the time. Restarting the application — even after a multi-day gap in this course's own work — picked the aggregation back up from exactly where it left off, rather than resetting to zero.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A KTable's current state is materialized into a local state store (RocksDB by default) on whichever machine is running that partition's processing — but critically, every update to that state store is also written to an internal changelog topic (visible directly: this app's is named streams-wordcount-KSTREAM-AGGREGATE-STATE-STORE-0000000003-changelog, a real topic this course's broker is genuinely holding). The local RocksDB store is a cache for fast reads; the changelog topic is the durable source of truth. When a Streams application starts (or restarts, on the same or even a different machine), it replays its changelog topic to rebuild local state before processing any new input — which is exactly why this lesson's counts resumed from 5 rather than starting over: the changelog topic had durably recorded "kafka" had already reached 4, and replaying it on startup reconstructed that state before the three new "kafka" occurrences were even counted.

This is the direct, practical payoff of treating a KTable as log-backed rather than purely in-memory: Streams applications get the same crash-recovery and rebalancing-safety story Kafka itself has for partition data (Level 1, Lesson 7) applied to application state, not just the raw input stream — a worker crashing and another instance picking up its partitions doesn't lose the aggregated counts, because they live in Kafka, not just in one process's memory.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting a Streams application's aggregated state to reset on restart. As this lesson shows directly (if accidentally), it doesn't by default — if you genuinely want a fresh start, you need to reset the application explicitly (the kafka-streams-application-reset tool, covered in Level 3's later lessons), not just restart the process.
  • Treating a KStream and the KTable its aggregation produces as the same kind of thing. They have fundamentally different semantics — a KStream has no concept of "updating" a prior record; a KTable is defined entirely around that concept.
  • Forgetting that changelog topics are real, resource-consuming Kafka topics. They retain data (by default, indefinitely, since they're typically compacted rather than time-retained) and count toward real disk and replication overhead on the cluster — not a free side effect of using the DSL's aggregation operators.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run any Kafka Streams aggregation example, note its current counts, then genuinely stop and restart the application (not just the consumer reading its output) and confirm the counts resume rather than reset — as this lesson's own, unplanned restart did. Then find the changelog topic for your app's state store with kafka-topics.sh --list and confirm its cleanup.policy is compact (Level 1, Lesson 9) rather than time-based deletion.

docs.title: 05 · Streams Stateful Operations & State Stores
docs.text: Lesson 4 showed a KTable's aggregated counts surviving a real restart because of a changelog topic. This lesson reads that changelog topic directly, independent of the application, to prove it genuinely is the full, standalone source of truth for the aggregation's state — not just an internal implementation detail you have to trust blindly.

docs.title: What a state store actually is
docs.text: Any stateful DSL operation — count(), reduce(), aggregate(), a windowed aggregation, a join needing to remember one side's records — needs somewhere to keep that state between records. That's a state store: by default, an embedded RocksDB instance local to the task processing that partition, chosen specifically because it's an efficient, embeddable key-value store that doesn't require running a separate database process. Every state store Kafka Streams manages is, by default, backed by a changelog topic — the mechanism Lesson 4 relied on for its unplanned restart-recovery story.

docs.title: Worked example: reading the changelog directly, bypassing the application entirely
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --list --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 | grep changelog
streams-wordcount-KSTREAM-AGGREGATE-STATE-STORE-0000000003-changelog

$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh \
    --topic streams-wordcount-KSTREAM-AGGREGATE-STATE-STORE-0000000003-changelog \
    --from-beginning --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --property print.key=true \
    --value-deserializer org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.LongDeserializer --max-messages 8
kafka         5
streams       2
fundamentals  1
kstream       1
and           1
ktable        1
kafka         6
kafka         7

(Real output from this course's lab broker — read with a plain console consumer, with no Streams application involved in this specific read at all.) This is exactly the same sequence of values Lesson 4's read of the actual output topic showed. That's not a coincidence of this particular example — for a simple aggregation like word count, the changelog topic and the externally-visible output topic end up carrying equivalent data, because the aggregation's result is the thing being both materialized to the state store and emitted downstream. Reading the changelog with a plain consumer, bypassing the Streams application and its RocksDB store entirely, still gives you the full, correct picture of "what does this KTable currently believe," which is the concrete proof that the changelog — not the local RocksDB files — is the real, durable source of truth.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When a Streams task updates its local RocksDB state store (incrementing a word's count, say), it also produces a record to that store's changelog topic recording the update, as part of the same processing step. This dual-write is what lets a completely fresh instance (a new machine, after state.dir is wiped, or after this lesson's own multi-day gap) rebuild an equivalent RocksDB store from scratch: on startup, the task reads its changelog topic from the beginning (or from a local checkpoint, if one survived) and replays every update into a blank RocksDB instance before resuming live processing — which is precisely the mechanism Lesson 4's surprising "kafka started at 5, not 1" result depended on.

This also explains why changelog topics default to compacted cleanup policy (Level 1, Lesson 9): a changelog only needs to retain the latest value for each key to successfully rebuild current state — the full history of every intermediate count isn't needed for recovery, only "what's the final value for this key right now," which is exactly log compaction's job.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating the local RocksDB directory as the real data and the changelog as a side effect. As demonstrated directly, it's the other way around: the changelog is durable and authoritative; RocksDB is a disposable, rebuildable local cache for fast reads.
  • Deleting a changelog topic manually to "clean up" a Streams application, without understanding this destroys the only durable record of that application's current aggregated state — any surviving or future instance rebuilding state from it will come up empty or inconsistent.
  • Assuming every state store's changelog content matches its downstream output topic exactly, as this lesson's simple word-count example happens to. For a windowed aggregation or a join, the changelog and any externally-emitted stream can diverge in format and content — this lesson's clean correspondence is a property of word count's particular simplicity, not a universal guarantee.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Find a stateful Kafka Streams application's changelog topic with kafka-topics.sh --list (look for the -changelog suffix) and read it directly with a plain console consumer, independent of the running application. Confirm the values you see match what the application itself reports as current state (through its output topic, a queryable state store, or logs) — direct, hands-on proof of where the real state actually lives.

docs.title: 06 · Streams Joins & Windowing
docs.text: "A 5-second window" sounds like it should mean "events within 5 seconds of each other end up together," and a real test in this lesson shows that's not quite right — two events sent one second apart landed in different windows, while two events sent seven seconds apart landed in the same window.

docs.title: Fixed time windows are calendar-aligned, not event-relative
docs.text: A TimeWindows.ofSizeWithNoGrace(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) window doesn't start counting from whenever the first event for a key arrives — it divides time into fixed-size buckets aligned to epoch time (Unix time zero), the same way clock-minutes are fixed regardless of when you personally start paying attention to the clock. An event's window is determined entirely by its own timestamp falling into one of these pre-existing, fixed buckets — two events can be logically "close together" in wall-clock time while still landing in different buckets, if a bucket boundary happens to fall between them.

docs.title: Worked example: a real windowed count, including a real boundary-straddling
docs.text:
KTable<Windowed<String>, Long> counts = source
    .groupByKey()
    .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeWithNoGrace(Duration.ofSeconds(5)))
    .count();

$ echo "a:event1" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic window-input ...
$ sleep 1
$ echo "a:event2" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic window-input ...
$ sleep 7
$ echo "a:event3" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic window-input ...

key=a windowStart=1792910100000 windowEnd=1792910105000 count=1   <- event1
key=a windowStart=1792910105000 windowEnd=1792910110000 count=1   <- event2 (different window!)
key=a windowStart=1792910100000 windowEnd=1792910105000 count=1   <- unchanged
key=a windowStart=1792910105000 windowEnd=1792910110000 count=2   <- event3 joined event2's window

(Real output from this course's lab broker.) event1 and event2, sent only about one second apart, landed in two different 5-second windows — [...100000, ...105000) and [...105000, ...110000) — because the fixed boundary at 105000 happened to fall between them. event3, sent a full seven seconds after event2, landed in the same window as event2 (count went from 1 to 2 for that window), because seven seconds later still fell before that window's own end boundary. The window boundaries were fixed the instant the topology started; every event's timestamp is simply sorted into whichever pre-existing bucket it falls into, with zero regard for how close together events feel relative to each other.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A KTable<Windowed<String>, Long> is keyed by a composite key: the original key ("a") plus the specific window instance it belongs to — which is exactly why the same key "a" can have multiple, independently tracked counts live simultaneously, one per window it has events in. Each window's aggregate is itself a KTable entry, materialized to a windowed state store backed by its own changelog (the same durability model from Lesson 5), with an additional retention period controlling how long old windows are kept around before being purged — important because, without that bound, a long-running application would accumulate an unbounded number of historical window entries.

Joins (not shown in this lesson's specific example, but built on the same time-awareness) extend this further: a KStream-KStream join also needs a window, because without one, "join records from these two streams" would have no sensible bound — should an event from ten minutes ago still be eligible to join against one arriving right now?
