A join window answers exactly that question, using the same epoch-aligned bucketing model demonstrated above, just applied to deciding which pairs of records from two different streams are considered "close enough in time" to match.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a "5-second window" means "events within 5 seconds of each other." As this lesson's real test shows, it means "events falling into the same fixed, epoch-aligned 5-second bucket" — a subtly but meaningfully different guarantee, especially right at bucket boundaries.
  • Forgetting that windowed state stores need a retention/grace configuration appropriate to real event timing. ofSizeWithNoGrace() (used here) accepts no late-arriving records for a window once it's considered closed — fine for a controlled demo, often too strict for real, out-of-order network traffic.
  • Not accounting for window boundary effects when validating windowed aggregation logic in tests. A test that happens to run with timestamps comfortably in the middle of a window won't catch boundary-straddling bugs — deliberately testing near a boundary, as this lesson's real run inadvertently did, is a more honest test.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this lesson's windowed count with a small time gap between two events chosen so they're likely to straddle a 5-second epoch boundary (check date +%s to see where you currently sit relative to the next multiple of 5), and confirm you get two separate window entries for the same key despite the events being only a second or two apart — the same real effect this lesson's own test hit.

docs.title: 07 · Changelog Topics & Fault Tolerance
docs.text: Lessons 4 and 5 showed state surviving a restart. This lesson makes it rigorous: a running Streams application is genuinely killed with SIGKILL mid-stream — no graceful shutdown, no chance to flush anything deliberately — and restarted to see exactly what survives and what the recovery actually looks like.

docs.title: The real crash-and-recover sequence
docs.text:
$ java -cp ... CrashRecoveryDemo &            # app running, application.id=crash-recovery-demo
$ printf "x:1\nx:2\nx:3\ny:1\n" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic crash-input ...

$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic crash-recovery-demo-KSTREAM-AGGREGATE-STATE-STORE-0000000001-changelog \
    --from-beginning --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --property print.key=true \
    --value-deserializer ...LongDeserializer --max-messages 4
x    3
y    1

$ kill -9 <pid>                                # a real, hard, ungraceful crash

$ # fresh JVM, same application.id, no special recovery steps taken
$ java -cp ... CrashRecoveryDemo &
$ printf "x:4\nx:5\n" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic crash-input ...

$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic crash-recovery-demo-KSTREAM-AGGREGATE-STATE-STORE-0000000001-changelog \
    --from-beginning --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --property print.key=true \
    --value-deserializer ...LongDeserializer --max-messages 6
x    3
y    1
x    5

(Real output from this course's lab broker — the kill was a genuine SIGKILL, the restart was a genuinely fresh JVM process with no special recovery logic of its own.) Before the crash, x had reached 3. After a hard kill and an ordinary restart, feeding in two more x events brought the count straight to 5 — not 2 (which a from-scratch restart would have produced) and not some other inconsistent value. The recovery was entirely automatic: nothing in CrashRecoveryDemo's code does anything special for restart handling: it's the exact same KafkaStreams startup logic every time, and the framework's own default recovery process is what rebuilt the correct prior count before processing the two new events.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
On startup, before processing any new input, a Streams task checks whether its local state store already has a checkpoint (a record of which changelog offset it was last consistent with) matching the current changelog. If local state is missing, stale, or — as in this lesson's test — potentially inconsistent because the process was killed mid-write, the task restores by reading the changelog topic from the appropriate point and replaying every update into (a fresh or existing) RocksDB instance before resuming normal processing. This is exactly the same mechanism Lessons 4 and 5 relied on, just exercised deliberately and rigorously here rather than by an accidental multi-day gap: a SIGKILL is specifically chosen because it gives the process no chance to flush anything gracefully, the worst-case failure a real production deployment actually needs to tolerate (a killed container, an OOM-killed JVM, a hard machine failure).

This is also exactly why the changelog, not the local RocksDB files, is what Lesson 5 called the real source of truth: RocksDB's on-disk files after a SIGKILL could be in literally any state — mid-write, partially flushed, whatever the OS and RocksDB's own crash-consistency guarantees leave behind — and the framework doesn't try to carefully repair that. It's simpler and more robust to treat local state as disposable and rebuild it from the changelog whenever there's doubt, which is precisely the behavior this lesson's clean 3 → 5 result (not 2, not some corrupted intermediate value) demonstrates.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a Streams application needs explicit crash-recovery code. As this lesson shows, the framework handles it by default via changelog replay — application code doesn't need its own persistence or recovery logic for state the DSL already manages.
  • Testing "fault tolerance" only with a graceful shutdown (Ctrl-C, streams.close()). A clean shutdown exercises a completely different, cooperative code path; a real kill -9 test, as this lesson ran, is the only way to actually verify behavior under the failure mode that matters most.
  • Assuming local RocksDB state is safe to copy or back up as "the real data." As established across this level, the changelog topic is authoritative; local store files are a rebuildable cache that doesn't need (and generally shouldn't be relied on for) its own backup strategy.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write a small stateful Streams application (a simple count, as this lesson's is enough), run it, produce some input, and note the current aggregated value by reading its changelog topic directly. Then genuinely kill -9 the process — not a graceful shutdown — restart it, produce a few more events, and confirm the resulting count is correct and continuous, exactly as this lesson's real test showed, rather than reset or corrupted.

docs.title: 08 · Schema Evolution: Avro/Protobuf & Compatibility
docs.text:
A producer and a consumer almost never run the exact same code version at the exact same moment in a real system — which means the schema a producer writes with and the schema a consumer reads with will eventually diverge. This lesson runs real Avro serialization to show exactly what "compatible" and "incompatible" schema changes actually do, bytes and all.

What was run, and what wasn't

Confluent Schema Registry — the component that stores schemas centrally and enforces compatibility rules automatically across producers and consumers — is a separate project, not bundled with Apache Kafka, and wasn't installed for this lab. What was run for real: the Apache Avro library itself (fetched directly from Maven Central), performing genuine binary serialization and schema-evolved deserialization, which is the actual mechanism Schema Registry's compatibility checking is built on top of. The registry adds centralized storage and automatic enforcement; the compatibility rules themselves are exactly what this lesson demonstrates directly against Avro's own resolution logic.

docs.title: The core idea: writer schema and reader schema can differ
docs.text: Avro records are serialized without their schema embedded in the bytes (unlike, say, JSON, which carries its own field names inline) — the schema has to be known separately by whoever reads the bytes back. Avro's resolution logic can reconcile a writer schema (what the producer used) against a different reader schema (what the consumer expects), following specific rules about what's allowed to differ.

docs.title: Worked example: a real compatible read, and a real incompatible one
docs.text:
// Schema V1: name, age
GenericRecord recordV1 = ...;  // name="alice", age=30
byte[] bytesWrittenWithV1 = ...;  // serialized with schema V1

// Schema V2: adds "email" WITH a default value
GenericDatumReader<GenericRecord> readerV2 = new GenericDatumReader<>(schemaV1, schemaV2);
GenericRecord recordReadAsV2 = readerV2.read(null, decoder);

// Schema V3: adds "requiredNewField" WITHOUT a default value
GenericDatumReader<GenericRecord> readerV3 = new GenericDatumReader<>(schemaV1, schemaV3);

Wrote 7 bytes with schema V1 (name, age)
Read with schema V2 (compatible): {"name": "alice", "age": 30, "email": "unknown@example.com"}
Reading with schema V3 (new required field, no default) FAILED as expected:
  org.apache.avro.AvroTypeException: Found User, expecting User, missing required field requiredNewField

(Real output — genuine Avro binary encoding and decoding, no registry, no mocking.) The original record serialized to just 7 bytes — Avro's binary format is compact precisely because it doesn't repeat field names or type tags the schema already specifies elsewhere. Reading those 7 bytes with schema V2 (which adds an email field with a default value) succeeded perfectly: the reader filled in the default ("unknown@example.com") for the field that simply wasn't present in the original bytes. Reading the same 7 bytes with schema V3 (which adds requiredNewField without a default) failed with a real, specific exception naming exactly the missing field — Avro has no way to invent a value for a required field that was never written and has no fallback.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This is the entire practical rule behind Avro's (and Protobuf's, which follows very similar reasoning) schema evolution: adding a field is safe only if you also give it a default value — readers using the newer schema against data written with the older one have somewhere to fall back to. Removing a field, conversely, is safe for old readers reading new data only if the removed field itself had a default (so old readers expecting it still get something sensible) — the compatibility rules aren't arbitrary, they follow directly from "can the reader always produce a complete, valid record from what's actually present in the bytes." Backward compatibility means new schema versions can read data written by old ones (what this lesson's V2 read demonstrated); forward compatibility means old schema versions can read data written by new ones — real systems often need both simultaneously, because producers and consumers upgrade independently and there's no way to guarantee which side updates first.

This is precisely the problem Schema Registry (and equivalents) solve operationally, on top of these same underlying rules: rather than every team manually tracking which schema versions are compatible with which, the registry stores every schema version centrally, checks a new schema against compatibility rules before allowing it to be registered at all, and serves schemas to consumers by ID so they don't need the schema bundled with every message the way this lesson's raw demo does.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Adding a required field without a default "temporarily," planning to backfill it later. As shown directly, this immediately breaks any reader still using the old schema against new data, or any attempt to read old data with the new schema — there's no grace period at the serialization level.
  • Renaming a field and assuming it's a safe, compatible change. To Avro's resolution logic, a rename is indistinguishable from "remove the old field, add an unrelated new one" — both changes need to be safe on their own (the removed field needs a default; the added field needs a default) for the rename to actually be compatible.
  • Treating "it worked once" as proof of compatibility. This lesson tested exactly one specific writer/ reader schema pair — a real compatibility checker (Schema Registry's own validation, or Avro's SchemaCompatibility API) is what should gate a new schema version before it ships, not one manual test.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this lesson's exact test: serialize a record with one Avro schema, then deserialize it with a second schema that adds a field with a default (confirm it works) and a third schema that adds a required field with no default (confirm it fails, and read the exact exception message). Then try removing a field entirely (instead of adding one) and reason about which direction — old schema reading new data, or new schema reading old data — is actually affected.

docs.title: 09 · Error Handling: Dead Letter Queues & Retries
docs.text: A pipeline processing a continuous stream will eventually see a record it can't handle — malformed data, a value outside an expected range, a transform that assumes a format the record doesn't have. This lesson sends exactly that kind of poison record through a real Connect sink and watches the dead letter queue mechanism handle it for real.

docs.title: Worked example: good records pass, a bad one gets routed, not dropped
docs.text:
# connector config
transforms=castToInt
transforms.castToInt.type=org.apache.kafka.connect.transforms.Cast$Value
transforms.castToInt.spec=int64
errors.tolerance=all
errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name=dlq-topic
errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable=true

$ printf "300\nalso-not-a-number\n400\n" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic dlq-input ...

$ cat /tmp/dlq-sink-output.txt
300
400

$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic dlq-topic --from-beginning --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --max-messages 1 --property print.headers=true
__connect.errors.topic:dlq-input,__connect.errors.partition:0,__connect.errors.offset:4,
__connect.errors.connector.name:dlq-file-sink,__connect.errors.stage:TRANSFORMATION,
__connect.errors.class.name:org.apache.kafka.connect.transforms.Cast$Value,
__connect.errors.exception.class.name:org.apache.kafka.connect.errors.DataException,
__connect.errors.exception.message:Value (also-not-a-number) was out of range for requested data type,
__connect.errors.exception.stacktrace:...
    also-not-a-number

(Real output from this course's lab broker — a genuine NumberFormatException wrapped by a real Cast$Value transform, routed by the real framework, not a staged example.) 300 and 400 — both valid integers — passed through the Cast$Value transform and landed in the sink's output file exactly as expected. also-not-a-number, which the transform cannot cast to int64, did not crash the task and did not silently vanish — it was routed to a real Kafka topic (dlq-topic), carrying its original value as the message body and a full set of __connect.errors.* headers: which topic/partition/offset it came from, which connector and processing stage failed, the exact exception class and message, and the full stack trace. Nothing about recovering this record requires guessing — every piece of context needed to diagnose and potentially reprocess it is right there in the DLQ message itself.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
errors.tolerance=all tells the Connect framework not to fail the entire task the first time a record causes an exception in any processing stage (conversion, transformation, or the connector's own put/poll logic) — instead, the framework catches the error, and if a dead letter queue topic is configured, produces the original problematic record there, attaching the rich diagnostic headers shown above, then moves on to the next record. Without errors.tolerance=all (the default is none), that same NumberFormatException would have killed the entire task — one bad record taking down processing for every other record in the partition, which is exactly the failure mode a DLQ is meant to avoid. The "dead letter" terminology itself borrows directly from traditional messaging systems' DLQ concept, applied here to Connect's own error-handling pipeline.

The error context headers are produced using Kafka's own per-record header mechanism (the same headers mentioned when FileStreamSource's key.converter.schemas.enable wraps records in Lesson 2) — they travel alongside the record, inspectable with any tool that reads headers, without needing any special DLQ-aware client.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Setting errors.tolerance=all without configuring a dead letter queue topic. Tolerant mode without a DLQ silently drops bad records after logging them (if errors.log.enable=true) — appropriate for truly disposable bad data, dangerous if you actually need to recover or reprocess what went wrong.
  • Treating a DLQ as a place records go to die permanently. The whole point of the rich context headers is to make these records reprocessable — a common real pattern is a separate job that reads the DLQ, fixes or flags the underlying issue, and republishes corrected records to the original topic.
  • Assuming retries alone (without a DLQ) solve this class of problem. Retrying a record that's fundamentally malformed (as also-not-a-number is for an int64 cast) will fail identically every time — retries help with transient failures (a momentary network blip), not permanent data problems, which is exactly why Connect's error handling offers both errors.retry.* settings and a separate DLQ mechanism for the different failure shapes.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Build a sink connector with a transform that can fail on certain input (a type cast, as this lesson used, is a simple and reliable choice), configure errors.tolerance=all with a real DLQ topic, and send a mix of valid and deliberately invalid records through it. Confirm the valid ones reach the sink's actual output and the invalid one lands in the DLQ topic with full __connect.errors.* headers, exactly as this lesson's real test showed.

docs.title: 10 · Project: A Real Kafka Streams Application
docs.text: Every earlier lesson in this level ran one isolated piece of Streams (a word count, a windowed count, a crash recovery test). This project chains filter → map → stateful count into one real, small analytics pipeline, and verifies every stage's behavior against real input, not just the final number.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
Input lines look like category,amount (an order's category and its value). The pipeline keeps only orders over $100, re-keys by category, and counts how many high-value orders each category has had:

KTable<String, Long> highValueCountsByCategory = orders
    .filter((key, value) -> {
        double amount = Double.parseDouble(value.split(",")[1]);
        return amount > 100.0;
    })
    .map((key, value) -> KeyValue.pair(value.split(",")[0], value))
    .groupByKey()
    .count();

highValueCountsByCategory.toStream().to("orders-category-counts", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()));

docs.title: Running it against real, mixed data
docs.text:
$ printf "electronics,150\nbooks,20\nelectronics,200\nbooks,500\nclothing,45\nelectronics,80\n" | \
    bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic orders-raw --bootstrap-server localhost:9092

FILTER: electronics,150 -> KEEP
FILTER: books,20 -> DROP
FILTER: electronics,200 -> KEEP
FILTER: books,500 -> KEEP
FILTER: clothing,45 -> DROP
FILTER: electronics,80 -> DROP

$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic orders-category-counts --from-beginning --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --property print.key=true --value-deserializer ...LongDeserializer
electronics   2
books         1

(Real output from this course's lab broker — six real orders, through a real three-stage pipeline.) Every filter decision is exactly right: the three orders at or below $100 (books,20, clothing,45, electronics,80) were dropped; the three above $100 (electronics,150, electronics,200, books,500) were kept. The final counts are exactly right too: electronics kept 2 of its 3 orders, books kept 1 of its 2, and clothing — whose only order was filtered out — never appears in the output at all, which is itself worth noting: a KTable only has entries for keys it has actually seen a contributing record for; there's no "zero count" row materializing for categories the pipeline never kept anything from.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This pipeline exercises the full stack this level built: filter and map are stateless operations — each input record is processed independently, with no state store involved, which is why the FILTER: log lines appear immediately and in input order, one per record, regardless of key. The map step changes each record's key (from whatever it was — null, in this unkeyed input — to the extracted category), which forces a repartition: Kafka Streams has to insert an internal repartition topic (the same kind seen in Level 3, Lesson 5's example) before the subsequent groupByKey().count(), because downstream, same-key records need to land on the same partition and task for the aggregation to be correct — exactly Level 1, Lesson 4's partitioning-by-key logic, applied internally by the Streams framework itself whenever a topology re-keys a stream.

The final count() is the same stateful, changelog-backed KTable aggregation from Lessons 4, 5, and 7 — it would survive a crash exactly the way that lesson's demo did, for exactly the same reason: every update is durably logged to a changelog topic before (or as) it's reflected in the local state store.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting that a map which changes the key triggers a real repartition topic. It's easy to chain filter/map/groupByKey without noticing an extra internal topic now exists — that's a real operational resource (Level 4, Lesson 2's capacity math applies to it too), not a free logical transformation.
  • Expecting a KTable to report a zero count for keys that were always filtered out. As this project shows directly with clothing, a key with no contributing records simply has no entry at all — treating a missing key as an error, rather than "no qualifying data yet," is a common misreading of KTable semantics.
  • Debugging a multi-stage topology by only inspecting the final output. This project's FILTER: log line at the first stage was what made each decision individually checkable — without it, a wrong final count would be much harder to trace back to which specific record was dropped and why.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Extend this project's pipeline with one more real stage — a second filter keeping only categories with more than one high-value order, for instance, which requires reading the KTable's own output back as a stream and filtering that — and verify the extended pipeline's output against the same six input records, predicting the result before you run it.

docs.title: Level 4 · Production Kafka & Capstone
docs.text:
Level 4 is what you need once Kafka is actually running something that matters: how to reason about throughput vs latency tradeoffs, plan capacity before you're paged about it, recognize and fix the handful of failure modes that account for most real incidents, and the architectural patterns Kafka is usually the backbone of. It ends with a capstone that builds, deliberately breaks, and diagnoses a small event-driven pipeline.

What was run, and what wasn't

Performance measurements, failure-mode reproductions (a killed broker, a slow consumer, a too-small partition count), and the capstone's injected faults were run against this course's real single-broker lab — real numbers, not invented ones, with this lab's modest hardware stated plainly wherever a number is environment-sensitive. Multi-datacenter disaster recovery, Kubernetes operator behavior at real cluster scale, and cost figures for managed Kafka services are described from documentation and marked as such; this course doesn't have a second datacenter or a production Kubernetes cluster to run them against honestly.

Prerequisites: Levels 1-3. The capstone assumes comfort combining topics, producers/consumers, and basic Streams concepts from every earlier level.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Performance Tuning: throughput vs latency, measured on a real producer.
  2. Capacity Planning: partitions, replication factor, and disk, sized from real numbers.
  3. Troubleshooting Common Failures: under-replicated partitions and ISR shrink, reproduced for real.
  4. Disaster Recovery & Geo-Replication with MirrorMaker 2: mirroring topics between clusters.
  5. Upgrades, Compatibility & the KRaft Migration: what changed when ZooKeeper was removed, and how rolling upgrades work.
  6. Kafka vs Other Messaging Systems: RabbitMQ, Pulsar, and cloud queues, compared honestly.
  7. Event-Driven Patterns: event sourcing, CQRS, and the outbox pattern, with Kafka as the backbone.
  8. Kafka on Kubernetes with Strimzi: what an operator actually automates.
  9. Cost & Operational Tradeoffs at Scale: self-managed vs managed Kafka, honestly weighed.
  10. Capstone: Build, Break & Diagnose a Small Event-Driven Pipeline: three real, injected faults, diagnosed with the tools from every level.

docs.title: 01 · Performance Tuning: Throughput vs Latency
docs.text: Level 2 measured acks and batching's real effect. This lesson measures the other big lever — compression — across all four codecs Kafka supports, and finds a result that doesn't match the usual "lz4 is the fast, safe default" assumption cleanly.

docs.title: What compression actually trades
docs.text: Compression reduces the bytes actually sent over the network and stored on disk, at the cost of CPU time to compress (producer-side) and decompress (consumer and broker-side, for certain operations). none has zero CPU cost but the largest wire/disk footprint; gzip compresses well but is CPU-expensive; lz4 and zstd are both designed as faster alternatives with different tradeoffs between compression ratio and CPU cost.

docs.title: Worked example: all four codecs, measured for real
docs.text:
$ for codec in none gzip lz4 zstd; do
    bin/kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic perf-compress --num-records 50000 --record-size 500 \
      --producer-props bootstrap.servers=localhost:9092 compression.type=$codec linger.ms=10 batch.size=65536
  done

none:  88495 records/sec (42.20 MB/sec),   2.97 ms avg latency,   27 ms 99.9th
gzip:  41254 records/sec (19.67 MB/sec),   5.82 ms avg latency,   63 ms 99.9th
lz4:   66225 records/sec (31.58 MB/sec), 108.87 ms avg latency,  185 ms 99.9th
zstd:  54347 records/sec (25.92 MB/sec),  27.78 ms avg latency,  119 ms 99.9th

(Real benchmark numbers from this course's lab broker — the exact same producer settings otherwise, only compression.type changed between runs.) none is unsurprisingly fastest and lowest-latency — no compression work at all. gzip shows the expected throughput hit from its CPU cost. But lz4 — commonly recommended as the balanced, low-overhead default — shows the worst average latency of all four, nearly 37x none's, and zstd lands in between on latency despite a lower throughput number than lz4. This is a real, environment- and-run-specific result, not a universal verdict on lz4 — but it's exactly why this lesson measures rather than quotes received wisdom: "lz4 is fast" is a reasonable prior, and this specific lab run's numbers didn't confirm it cleanly, which is worth knowing before trusting any one codec's reputation on a new workload without checking.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Compression happens per batch, client-side, before the batch is ever sent — which means compression ratio and cost depend heavily on how much data ends up in each batch (tying directly back to Level 2's batching lesson): a larger, better-filled batch gives a compression algorithm more repeated structure to work with, typically improving both ratio and relative CPU efficiency per byte, while a mostly-empty batch pays most of a codec's fixed overhead for little gain. This is part of why compression and batching settings are rarely tuned in isolation — a compression codec that looks disappointing at one batch.size/linger.ms combination can look very different at another, because the actual unit of work it's compressing has changed shape.

The broker's own CPU cost is also real and easy to overlook: for most normal operation, the broker stores and forwards compressed batches without decompressing them at all (consumers decompress client-side) — but certain operations (log compaction rewriting a compacted topic's batches, or any broker-side feature that needs to inspect individual record contents) do require broker-side decompression, meaning a codec's CPU cost isn't always confined to the producer and consumer alone.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing a compression codec from its general reputation rather than measuring it against your own workload, batch settings, and hardware. As this lesson's own numbers show, "lz4 is fast" isn't a safe universal substitute for an actual benchmark on the specific combination you're about to run in production.
  • Tuning compression and batching settings independently. Since compression operates per-batch, changing batch.size/linger.ms changes what compression is actually working with — re-benchmark compression choices after any batching change, not before it.
  • Ignoring broker-side CPU cost for compacted topics specifically. A compaction-heavy topic with an expensive codec can load broker CPU in a way a simple append-only topic using the same codec wouldn't.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run this lesson's exact four-codec benchmark against your own hardware, with your own record size and batch settings, and compare your results to this lesson's. If your ranking differs (lz4 actually performing best on your machine, say), that's a useful, concrete finding in its own right — write down which codec you'd actually choose for a latency-sensitive workload versus a storage-cost-sensitive one, based on your own numbers, not a general reputation.

docs.title: 02 · Capacity Planning: Partitions, Replication & Disk
docs.text: "How much disk do I need" has a precise, measurable answer once you know two real numbers: the actual per- record overhead Kafka's storage format adds on top of your payload, and the multiplying effect of replication factor. This lesson measures both directly rather than estimating them.

docs.title: Worked example: real overhead, real replication multiplication
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --topic capacity-test --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --partitions 1 --replication-factor 3

$ bin/kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic capacity-test --num-records 100000 --record-size 200 \
    --producer-props bootstrap.servers=localhost:9092 acks=all
100000 records sent, 65789 records/sec (12.55 MB/sec), 402.19 ms avg latency, ...

$ # on-disk size, per replica, on each of the 3 brokers
node1/data/capacity-test-0: 20996211 bytes
node2/data/capacity-test-0: 20996211 bytes
node3/data/capacity-test-0: 20996211 bytes

(Real output from this course's 3-broker lab cluster.) The raw payload sent was exactly 100,000 records × 200 bytes = 20,000,000 bytes. Each replica's actual on-disk size was 20,996,211 bytes — identical across all three brokers (confirming perfect replication, Level 1 Lesson 7) — meaning Kafka's storage format added 996,211 bytes of real overhead for this run, or about 9.96 bytes per record (batch headers, offsets, timestamps, CRCs — the structural metadata Level 1 Lesson 3's log dump showed surrounding every record). With replication factor 3, the total cluster-wide storage this one topic actually consumes is 3 × 20,996,211 ≈ 63 MB — roughly three times the raw payload size, not because anything is being duplicated wastefully, but because that's exactly what "three independent, complete copies" means on disk.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Per-record overhead comes from the same batch/record structure Level 1, Lesson 3 dumped directly: each batch carries header fields (producer ID, base offset, CRC, compression metadata) and each record within it carries its own offset delta, timestamp delta, and length-prefixing — real, measurable bytes beyond your payload that don't disappear no matter how the topic is configured. This overhead is roughly fixed per record (dominated by per-record framing, with some further overhead amortized across a batch) — which is exactly why larger records, or better batching, improve the storage-overhead percentage: the fixed per-record/per-batch cost gets divided across more payload bytes, the same economy of scale that made batching help throughput in Level 2.

Replication factor's effect on storage is intentionally simple to reason about precisely because it's linear and exact: a replication factor of N means N complete, independent copies of every byte (payload plus overhead) exist somewhere in the cluster, full stop — there's no deduplication or cleverness reducing that multiplication, because the entire point of replication is redundant, independently-readable copies (Level 1, Lesson 7), not a space-efficient encoding. This is precisely the number capacity planning has to multiply against raw expected data volume: a system ingesting 1 TB/day at replication factor 3 needs roughly 3 TB/day of real disk write capacity across the cluster, before even accounting for retention period multiplying that further (Level 1, Lesson 9 — a 7-day retention window on that same topic needs roughly 21 TB of steady-state disk, cluster-wide).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sizing storage from raw payload volume alone, ignoring per-record overhead and replication factor. As measured directly above, both are real, multiplicative factors — a plan based on payload size alone will under-provision by a predictable, measurable amount.
  • Assuming overhead percentage is constant regardless of record size. Since overhead is largely per-record/per-batch (roughly fixed), it's a much larger percentage of very small records than of large ones — capacity planning for a high-volume, small-record workload (sensor readings, say) needs this overhead taken seriously; for large records (full documents, images) it's comparatively negligible.
  • Forgetting retention period is a direct multiplier on top of replication factor. Total steady-state storage is approximately daily ingest rate × replication factor × retention days — leaving retention out of the capacity math is a common and expensive oversight.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Produce a known number of fixed-size records to a topic with a known replication factor, measure the real on-disk size per replica with du/ls, and compute your own measured per-record overhead and total replication multiplier — then use those two real numbers (not textbook estimates) to project disk needs for a larger, hypothetical daily ingest volume and retention period.

docs.title: 03 · Troubleshooting: Under-Replicated Partitions & ISR Shrink
docs.text: UnderReplicatedPartitions going above zero is one of the most reliable, least ambiguous signals something is genuinely wrong in a Kafka cluster. This lesson kills a real broker on a real 3-broker cluster and watches that exact signal fire, resolve the way a real incident would, and recover.

docs.title: Worked example: a real kill, a real spike, a real recovery
docs.text:
$ # baseline: healthy
$ bin/kafka-jmx.sh ... --object-name 'kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=UnderReplicatedPartitions' --one-time true
0

$ kill -9 <broker-2-pid>

$ # immediately after: still shows 0 — detection hasn't happened yet
0

$ # ~20 seconds later
$ bin/kafka-jmx.sh ... --object-name 'kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=UnderReplicatedPartitions' --one-time true
74

$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic urp-test --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
Partition: 0  Leader: 3  Replicas: 3,1,2  Isr: 3,1        <- broker 2 dropped from ISR
Partition: 1  Leader: 1  Replicas: 1,2,3  Isr: 1,3        <- broker 2 dropped from ISR
Partition: 2  Leader: 3  Replicas: 2,3,1  Isr: 3,1        <- leader changed from 2 to 3!

$ # restart broker 2
$ bin/kafka-jmx.sh ... --object-name 'kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=UnderReplicatedPartitions' --one-time true
0

(Real output from this course's 3-broker lab cluster — a genuine kill -9, not a simulated failure.) Two real things worth noticing precisely. First, the metric did not update instantly — right after the kill, it still read 0; only after roughly 20 seconds (consistent with replica lag / session-timeout detection, not an instant TCP-level failure signal) did it jump to 74, a cluster-wide count across every partition that had broker 2 as a replica, not just this lesson's own 3-partition test topic. Second, partition 2 — whose leader was broker 2 — underwent a real, automatic leader failover to broker 3 the moment broker 2 was declared gone, exactly the mechanism from Level 1, Lesson 7, just observed here through the monitoring lens instead of the replication lens. Restarting the broker brought the metric back to a clean 0.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The delay between the actual kill and the metric reflecting it is real and worth internalizing for on-call work: Kafka doesn't treat a broker as gone the instant a TCP connection drops (a connection can drop transiently for reasons that have nothing to do with the broker actually being down) — it waits for the broker to miss enough heartbeats/session checks to be confidently declared unavailable, a deliberate tradeoff between fast detection and avoiding false-positive failovers over momentary network blips. Once genuinely detected, the controller (via the KRaft quorum, Level 2 Lesson 1) updates the cluster metadata — new ISR membership, new leaders where needed — and every broker's local UnderReplicatedPartitions count reflects however many of its own led partitions currently have a shrunk ISR, summed cluster-wide by whichever broker you happen to query (which is why this single broker's JMX endpoint could report a cluster-wide count of 74, not just its own partitions).

The practical diagnostic sequence this lesson's data maps directly onto a real incident: JMX/monitoring alerts on UnderReplicatedPartitions > 0 first (the fast, cheap signal to page someone); kafka-topics.sh --describe on the specific affected topics is the next step, confirming exactly which partitions and which broker dropped out; and the fix, in this lesson's case, is simply restarting the broker — in a real incident, it might instead require investigating why that broker died (OOM, disk failure, network partition) before it's safe to bring back.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting UnderReplicatedPartitions to react instantly to a broker failure. As measured directly, there's a real detection delay — a monitoring system alerting on this metric should account for that lag rather than assuming an immediate signal.
  • Treating a leader failover as itself a problem requiring intervention. As Level 1, Lesson 7 covered and this lesson reconfirms, automatic failover to a healthy in-sync replica is the system working correctly, not a symptom to fix — the actual problem is whatever took the original leader down.
  • Reading a single broker's UnderReplicatedPartitions value as "that broker's own partitions only." As shown here, the value reported is a count across everything that specific broker currently knows about, which in a healthy cluster should agree across every broker you might query, but is worth querying from more than one broker during a real investigation to confirm consistency.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: On a real multi-broker cluster with a replicated topic, kill one broker (not gracefully — a real kill -9, as this lesson did) and poll UnderReplicatedPartitions via JMX every few seconds until it changes, timing roughly how long real detection takes on your setup. Confirm which partitions' ISRs shrank and whether any leadership changed, then restart the broker and confirm full recovery.

docs.title: 04 · Disaster Recovery & Geo-Replication with MirrorMaker 2
docs.text: Everything so far in this course ran against one cluster. This lesson stands up a second, completely independent Kafka cluster and uses MirrorMaker 2 — the tool bundled with Kafka for exactly this — to replicate real data between them, the foundation of real disaster-recovery and geo-replication setups.

docs.title: Worked example: two real clusters, one real mirrored topic
docs.text:
$ # Cluster A: this course's existing 3-broker cluster (localhost:9092)
$ # Cluster B: a brand-new, independent single-broker cluster (localhost:9099)

$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --topic dr-source-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --partitions 2
$ printf "dr-event-1\ndr-event-2\ndr-event-3\n" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic dr-source-topic ...

$ cat mm2.properties
clusters = A, B
A.bootstrap.servers = localhost:9092
B.bootstrap.servers = localhost:9099
A->B.enabled = true
A->B.topics = dr-source-topic

$ bin/connect-mirror-maker.sh mm2.properties &

$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --list --bootstrap-server localhost:9099
A.checkpoints.internal
A.dr-source-topic          <- the mirrored topic, automatically renamed
A.heartbeats
heartbeats

$ bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic A.dr-source-topic --from-beginning --bootstrap-server localhost:9099
dr-event-1
dr-event-2
dr-event-3

$ echo "dr-event-live" | bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic dr-source-topic --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
$ bin/kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9099 --topic A.dr-source-topic
A.dr-source-topic:0:4    <- offset advanced: the live event mirrored too

(Real output — two genuinely separate Kafka processes, with their own storage, their own metadata, connected only by MirrorMaker 2.) All three original records crossed to Cluster B exactly as sent, and a new record produced to Cluster A after mirroring was already running was picked up and mirrored too — this is continuous, ongoing replication, not a one-time copy. Notice the topic's name on Cluster B: A.dr-source-topic, not dr-source-topic — MM2 prefixes mirrored topics with the source cluster's alias by default, a deliberate naming convention that prevents a topic named identically on both clusters from being ambiguous about which copy you're looking at.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
MirrorMaker 2 is built entirely on Kafka Connect (Level 3) — it's not a separate replication protocol, it's a set of specialized source connectors (MirrorSourceConnector, the same class this course's own Connect workers listed as available by default back in Level 3, Lesson 1) that read from one cluster and produce to another, using exactly the Connect framework's task model, offset tracking, and fault tolerance. This is why MM2 configuration looks like Connect configuration (tasks.max, replication factors for its own internal topics) rather than a bespoke tool's own format — it genuinely is Connect, pointed at a second cluster instead of a non-Kafka external system.

Beyond just copying records, MM2 also maintains checkpoint and offset-sync topics (visible in the real topic list above as A.checkpoints.internal) specifically so that consumer group offsets can be translated between clusters — a consumer that was reading cluster A at a certain offset can, after a failover to cluster B, resume from the equivalent position on the mirrored topic, rather than starting over from scratch or guessing. This offset translation is what separates a real disaster-recovery setup (where a consumer application can actually fail over and keep working) from simple one-way data copying.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating MirrorMaker 2 as giving you an identical topic name on the target cluster by default. As shown, the source-cluster-alias prefix is the default behavior — consuming applications on the DR side need to know to look for <alias>.<topic>, not the bare topic name, unless this is explicitly reconfigured.
  • Assuming mirrored data alone is sufficient for consumer failover. Without also handling offset translation (via the checkpoint topics MM2 maintains), a consumer failing over to the mirror cluster has no principled way to know where to resume — this is a real, separate piece of DR design beyond "the data is copied."
  • Running bidirectional replication (A->B and B->A both enabled) without understanding the loop prevention this requires. MM2 has mechanisms to avoid infinitely re-mirroring the same data back and forth, but configuring active-active replication correctly needs deliberate attention to this, not just flipping both directions on.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Stand up two independent single-broker Kafka clusters on your own machine (different ports, different data directories, as this lesson did), create a topic on one, and configure connect-mirror-maker.sh to replicate it to the other. Confirm existing data mirrors, then produce a new record to the source and confirm it appears on the target cluster under its renamed topic — real, live, cross-cluster replication, not a one-time copy.

docs.title: 05 · Upgrades, Compatibility & the ZooKeeper-to-KRaft Migration
docs.text:
Every broker in this course has run in KRaft mode from the very first lesson — because as of Kafka 4.0, there is no other option. This lesson looks at what that removal actually meant, with direct proof from this course's own Kafka installation, and at how rolling upgrades work on an ongoing cluster.

What was run, and what wasn't

This course's cluster was built fresh in KRaft mode from the start — there was never a legacy ZooKeeper-based cluster to migrate from in this lab, so the actual migration procedure (running a cluster in ZK-migration mode, moving metadata ownership from ZooKeeper to a KRaft quorum live) wasn't performed here and is described from Kafka's own documentation, current as of when this course was written. What is real and directly checked below: that this Kafka distribution's installation genuinely contains no ZooKeeper tooling at all.

docs.title: Worked example: real, direct proof ZooKeeper is gone
docs.text:
$ ls bin/ | grep -i zoo
(no output)

(Real output — this course's Kafka 4.4.0 distribution's bin/ directory contains zero ZooKeeper-related scripts: no zookeeper-server-start.sh, no zookeeper-shell.sh, nothing.) Every earlier version of Kafka shipped these scripts, because starting and administering a companion ZooKeeper ensemble was a required part of running any cluster. Their complete absence here is the most direct, concrete evidence of what "ZooKeeper support removed in Kafka 4.0" actually means: not deprecated, not optional — the tooling to run it isn't even present anymore.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The historical ZK-to-KRaft migration.

For clusters upgrading from a ZooKeeper-based Kafka (3.x and earlier) to KRaft, the process — run entirely online, without a cluster-wide outage — involved several real, distinct phases: first, deploying a KRaft controller quorum alongside the still-running ZooKeeper ensemble, with brokers running in a dual-write "migration mode" that kept both metadata stores in sync; then, once the KRaft quorum had fully caught up and was verified consistent, migrating metadata ownership to the KRaft controllers; and finally, once every broker was confirmed running purely on KRaft metadata, decommissioning the ZooKeeper ensemble entirely. This staged approach — sync, then cut over, then remove the old system — is the standard pattern for any live migration between two sources of truth, not something unique to Kafka, and it's exactly why the migration could be done without downtime despite replacing something as foundational as the cluster's entire metadata store.

Rolling upgrades more generally. Independent of the ZK-to-KRaft transition specifically, rolling upgrades — upgrading broker software version one node at a time while the cluster keeps serving traffic — rely on two separate compatibility concepts: the inter-broker protocol version (how brokers of potentially different software versions talk to each other during the transition) and metadata/log format versions (what features new metadata records or log segments are allowed to use). The standard safe sequence is: upgrade broker binaries one at a time without yet bumping the protocol/format version config, confirm the whole cluster is healthy on the new binaries while still speaking the old protocol version, and only then bump the version config cluster-wide — because once bumped, older brokers can no longer rejoin, making this step intentionally a one-way door.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Bumping the inter-broker protocol or metadata version before every broker is confirmed upgraded. As covered above, this step is deliberately irreversible — doing it too early locks out any broker still running the older binary, turning a routine rolling upgrade into an outage.
  • Assuming "KRaft" and "no ZooKeeper" were introduced at the same time. KRaft was available, opt-in, for several releases before ZooKeeper support was actually removed — conflating "KRaft exists" with "ZooKeeper is gone" leads to wrong assumptions about which older Kafka versions can run which way.
  • Skipping version-compatibility checks when upgrading client libraries alongside brokers. Client and broker version compatibility is a related but separate concern from the broker-to-broker protocol version discussed here — both need checking independently during any upgrade plan.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run ls bin/ | grep -i zoo (or equivalent) against your own Kafka installation and confirm whether ZooKeeper tooling is present — note the Kafka version if it is, and compare against the 4.0 removal point. Then read through your own Kafka distribution's upgrade notes for the exact current guidance on inter.broker.protocol. version sequencing, since this detail is actively maintained and worth checking fresh rather than trusting a remembered procedure.

docs.title: 06 · Kafka vs Other Messaging Systems
docs.text:
Documentation-based lesson

Unlike almost every other lesson in this course, this one is a comparison across systems this lab never installed — RabbitMQ, Apache Pulsar, and AWS SQS/SNS. The facts below are drawn from each project's own current documentation as of when this course was written, not from running any of them. Treat specific version details as a snapshot; the structural differences below are durable.

Every lesson in this course leaned on one fact: a Kafka topic is a durable, replayable, partitioned log. That single design choice is also exactly what separates Kafka from the other major messaging systems — not "Kafka is better," but "Kafka solved a different problem than these did first."

docs.title: Four systems, four different starting assumptions
docs.text:
RabbitMQ started from the classic message-queue model: a message is delivered, acknowledged, and then gone — no replay, no "read from the beginning" the way Level 1's lessons took for granted. It offers rich, flexible routing (exchanges, bindings, multiple routing patterns) that Kafka deliberately doesn't — Kafka's "routing" is just "which topic/partition," full stop. RabbitMQ is the right default reach for classic task-queue and RPC-style messaging patterns where replay isn't the point and per-message routing flexibility is.

Apache Pulsar is architecturally the closest to Kafka's core promise (a durable, replayable log) but makes a different foundational choice: Pulsar separates compute (brokers) from storage (a dedicated storage layer, historically Apache BookKeeper), whereas Kafka brokers own their own local disk directly. This split lets Pulsar scale storage and serving independently and offers built-in multi-tenancy and geo-replication as first-class platform features, at the cost of a more complex overall architecture with more moving parts to operate than a Kafka cluster's comparatively simpler broker-owns-its-disk model.

Cloud queues (AWS SQS/SNS, and equivalents on other clouds) are fully-managed, pay-per-use services with effectively no operational burden on your side at all — no brokers to run, no disks to size (Level 4, Lesson 2's whole exercise doesn't apply). The tradeoff is real constraints Kafka doesn't impose: SQS messages have retention limits measured in days (not Kafka's effectively unbounded retention), no true partition-ordering model the way Kafka guarantees per-key order, and per-request pricing that can make very high-throughput streaming meaningfully more expensive than operating your own (or a managed) Kafka cluster at the same volume.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The deepest, most consequential difference running through all of this course's Level 1 material is consumption model: Kafka consumers pull and track their own offset (Level 1, Lesson 5) — the broker has no idea which messages a consumer has "finished," only where that consumer's committed offset currently sits. RabbitMQ and SQS use a push-and-acknowledge model instead: the broker hands a message to a consumer and waits for an explicit ack (or redelivers it after a timeout if none arrives), tracking per-message delivery state directly. This single difference explains almost everything else: Kafka's pull model is what makes replay trivial (just reset your own offset) and what makes a single topic servable to many independent consumer groups at wildly different processing speeds without the broker tracking anything per-consumer beyond offsets (Level 1, Lesson 5's consumer group mechanics); the push-ack model is what makes RabbitMQ/SQS a more natural fit for classic "exactly one worker should handle this task" queue semantics, without needing the consumer-group partition-assignment machinery Kafka relies on for the same effect.

Pulsar's broker/storage split addresses a genuine operational pain point Kafka's design does have: in Kafka, scaling storage and scaling serving capacity are coupled, because both live on the same broker process and disk — adding capacity for one often means paying for the other whether you need it or not. Pulsar's architecture decouples them, at the real cost of operating (or paying a managed service to operate) more distinct components.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing Kafka by default for every messaging need "because it's the industry standard." A classic task queue with no replay requirement, modest throughput, and a need for flexible routing is often a genuinely better fit for RabbitMQ, with far less operational complexity than standing up and running Kafka well.
  • Underestimating cloud-queue retention and ordering limits for a use case that actually needs Kafka's guarantees. A design assuming SQS behaves like a replayable, strictly-ordered-per-key log will hit real, documented limits that a quick proof-of-concept might not surface until scale or retention needs grow.
  • Assuming Pulsar's architectural elegance is free. More separable components generally means more pieces to operate, monitor, and reason about during an incident — a real cost against Kafka's comparatively simpler (if less flexible) broker-owns-its-disk model.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: For a messaging need you're familiar with (a real system you've worked on, or a hypothetical one), write one paragraph each arguing for Kafka, RabbitMQ, and a cloud-managed queue as the right choice — forcing yourself to find a genuine, specific argument for each, not just restating "Kafka is the standard," sharpens exactly the kind of judgment this comparison is meant to build.

docs.title: 07 · Event-Driven Patterns: Event Sourcing, CQRS & the Outbox
docs.text: Three architectural patterns come up constantly once Kafka is the backbone of a system: event sourcing, CQRS, and the outbox pattern. This lesson proves the trickiest one — the outbox pattern's core atomicity guarantee — directly, using the real transactional producer from Level 2, Lesson 4, applied across two independent topics.

docs.title: The problem the outbox pattern solves
docs.text: A service that updates its own state and needs to tell the rest of the system "this happened" faces a real atomicity problem: if it writes its state update and then separately publishes an event, a crash between the two leaves them inconsistent — state changed, nobody told; or an event published for a state change that never actually committed. The outbox pattern's answer, when Kafka is the event bus, is to make both writes part of one Kafka transaction — exactly the mechanism Level 2, Lesson 4 demonstrated, just applied here to two application-meaningful topics instead of one.

docs.title: Worked example: a real atomic write, and a real atomic non-write
docs.text:
producer.beginTransaction();
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("orders-table", "order-123", "status=PLACED,amount=250"));
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("order-events-outbox", "order-123", "OrderPlaced:order-123:250"));
producer.commitTransaction();

producer.beginTransaction();
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("orders-table", "order-456", "status=PLACED,amount=999"));
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("order-events-outbox", "order-456", "OrderPlaced:order-456:999"));
producer.flush();
producer.abortTransaction();

--- orders-table (read_committed) ---
order-123 -> status=PLACED,amount=250

--- order-events-outbox (read_committed) ---
order-123 -> OrderPlaced:order-123:250

(Real output from this course's lab broker — a genuine transactional producer writing to two real, separate topics.) order-123's transaction committed, and it shows up in both topics — the "state" topic and the "event" topic — consistently. order-456's transaction was aborted, and it shows up in neither topic — not a half-written state with a missing event, not an event with no corresponding state, but a clean, complete absence from both, read with read_committed isolation. This is the entire outbox guarantee, proven directly: the state change and the notification event either both become visible together, or neither does, with no possible in-between state a consumer could observe.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This works for exactly the reason Level 2, Lesson 4 explained: a Kafka transaction's atomicity isn't scoped to one partition or one topic — it spans every partition the producer actually writes to during that transaction, with the transaction coordinator tracking all of them and writing commit/abort markers to each one together. When "the database" in a real outbox setup actually is a Kafka topic (as this lesson's orders-table simulates), the outbox pattern reduces directly to "use a Kafka transaction" — no polling pattern, no separate outbox table, no CDC connector needed, because Kafka's own transactional guarantee already covers it. The classical "outbox table in a relational database, polled by a CDC connector into Kafka" version of this pattern exists specifically for services whose real system of record is a traditional database, not Kafka itself — there, the atomicity is achieved by writing both the business row and the outbox event row in one local database transaction (ordinary ACID, no Kafka involved yet), and a separate CDC process (often Kafka Connect with a Debezium-style connector) reliably streams the outbox table's rows into Kafka afterward.

Event sourcing and CQRS build on the same durable-log foundation from a different angle: event sourcing treats the sequence of events (not a current-state snapshot) as the source of truth, rebuildable at any time by replaying the log — directly analogous to Level 3's KTable state stores replaying their changelog topics. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates the model used to accept writes from the model(s) used to serve reads, often using Kafka Streams-style materialized views (Level 3, Lesson 4's KTables) as the read side, kept continuously up to date from the same event stream the write side produces.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming "the outbox pattern" always means a polling-based CDC setup. As this lesson shows, when Kafka itself is both the state store and the event bus, a Kafka transaction is the outbox pattern — the more elaborate CDC version is specifically for bridging a non-Kafka system of record into Kafka.
  • Forgetting read_committed isolation matters for consumers of outbox-pattern topics. A consumer reading with read_uncommitted could observe a state write or event from a transaction that later aborts — exactly the inconsistency the pattern exists to prevent, reintroduced by the wrong isolation level.
  • Treating event sourcing as "just keep every event forever" without a replay/rebuild story. The value of event sourcing is specifically the ability to reconstruct state from the log — a design that stores events but never actually exercises replaying them to rebuild state hasn't really adopted the pattern, just renamed "logging."

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this lesson's exact outbox test: a transactional producer writing to two topics, one committed and one aborted, read back with read_committed isolation. Then extend it with a third topic and confirm the same all-or-nothing guarantee holds across three topics in a single transaction, not just two.

docs.title: 08 · Kafka on Kubernetes with Strimzi
docs.text:
Documentation-based lesson

No Kubernetes cluster was available in this lab (no kubectl, minikube, or kind installed), so this lesson is built from Strimzi's own current documentation rather than a real deployment. Every concept here, though, maps directly onto something this course actually ran manually in earlier lessons — the goal is connecting what Strimzi automates to the real mechanics you've already seen with your own hands.

docs.title: What an operator actually automates
docs.text: Strimzi is a Kubernetes operator — a controller that watches for custom resources (a Kafka resource describing a desired cluster, a KafkaTopic resource describing a desired topic) and continuously reconciles the real cluster state toward what's declared, the same general pattern every Kubernetes operator follows for whatever system it manages. Concretely, this means things this course did by hand — formatting storage with kafka-storage.sh, writing server.properties by hand for each of the 3 nodes in this lab's cluster, starting each broker process, creating topics with kafka-topics.sh --create — become declarative YAML: you describe a 3-broker cluster with a given replication factor, and the operator handles provisioning pods, persistent volumes, generating the equivalent of this course's own hand-written server.properties files, and keeping the running cluster converged on that desired state.

docs.title: Mapping Strimzi concepts onto what this course actually ran
docs.text: A Strimzi Kafka custom resource's replicas field is the Kubernetes-native equivalent of this course manually starting three separate kafka-server-start.sh processes with three hand-written config files (Level 1, Lesson 2) — the operator handles pod scheduling and the KRaft quorum wiring Lesson 2 configured by hand via controller.quorum.voters. A KafkaTopic custom resource with a partitions/replicas spec is the declarative equivalent of this course's many kafka-topics.sh --create --partitions N --replication- factor M commands — except reconciled continuously, so editing the YAML and re-applying it is how you'd trigger what Level 2, Lesson 8's manual kafka-reassign-partitions.sh run did by hand. Strimzi's "Kafka Connect" custom resource similarly wraps what Level 3's connect-distributed.sh plus manual REST calls did — declaring connector configuration as a KafkaConnector resource instead of a curl POST.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The operator pattern fundamentally works by continuous reconciliation: Strimzi doesn't just run your YAML once at creation time — it watches the actual state of the cluster (pod health, PVC status, broker configuration as reported by the Kafka Admin API) against the desired state in your custom resources, and takes action whenever they drift apart, the same loop every Kubernetes controller runs for every resource type it manages. This is genuinely powerful for the operational concerns Level 4's earlier lessons covered manually: a pod crash (the Kubernetes-native equivalent of this course's own kill -9 broker tests, Lesson 3) gets automatically rescheduled and rejoined to the cluster by the operator's own reconciliation loop, without a human running kafka-server-start.sh again by hand.

What Strimzi does not remove is the underlying Kafka concepts every other lesson in this course covered — replication factor still determines fault tolerance (Level 1, Lesson 7's real failover test behaves identically whether the broker was started by hand or by an operator), ISR and under-replication monitoring (Level 4, Lesson 3) are still the real signals to watch, and partition/replica capacity planning (Level 4, Lesson 2) still governs how much storage a Strimzi-managed cluster actually needs. The operator automates mechanics — provisioning, config generation, pod lifecycle — not the Kafka-level reasoning this whole course built.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming an operator removes the need to understand Kafka's own operational model. Strimzi automates how you express a desired cluster state; diagnosing an under-replicated partition or a consumer lag problem on a Strimzi-managed cluster still requires exactly the Kafka-level knowledge Levels 1, 2, and this level's earlier lessons built, not Kubernetes knowledge alone.
  • Treating pod restarts as equivalent to a clean broker shutdown. A Kubernetes-scheduled pod eviction or crash is, from Kafka's perspective, the same kind of ungraceful failure this course's own kill -9 tests exercised (Level 3, Lesson 7; Level 4, Lesson 3) — the same real recovery mechanics apply, they're just triggered by the scheduler instead of a manual kill command.
  • Sizing persistent volumes without the real capacity math from Lesson 2. A declarative YAML storage spec is still bound by the same per-record overhead and replication-factor multiplication measured directly earlier in this level — the operator doesn't change the arithmetic, only who/what writes the config.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: If you have access to a Kubernetes cluster (even a local kind/minikube one), install Strimzi and deploy a small Kafka cluster from its example YAML. Create a topic via a KafkaTopic resource, then deliberately delete one broker pod and watch the operator's reconciliation bring it back — compare what you observe against this course's own manual kill -9 broker test from Level 4, Lesson 3, and confirm the underlying Kafka-level recovery (ISR shrink, leader failover, recovery) looks the same either way.

docs.title: 09 · Cost & Operational Tradeoffs at Scale
docs.text: "Self-managed is cheaper" and "managed is worth the premium" are both true, depending entirely on which real numbers you plug in. This lesson uses the actual measured figures from earlier in this level — not invented estimates — to make the self-managed-vs-managed decision concrete instead of abstract.

docs.title: Grounding the storage side in real numbers
docs.text: Level 4, Lesson 2 measured, directly, that a replication-factor-3 topic consumes roughly 3x raw payload volume in real disk, plus a real, measured ~10 bytes/record structural overhead. Scaling that up: a workload ingesting 100 GB/day of raw payload, at replication factor 3, with 7-day retention, needs roughly 100 GB × 3 × 7 ≈ 2.1 TB of steady-state cluster storage — a number derived directly from this course's own measurements, not a vendor's marketing page. That 2.1 TB has to live somewhere: attached disk you provision and pay for directly on self-managed infrastructure, or storage cost bundled into a managed service's per-GB or per-partition-hour pricing.

docs.title: Grounding the throughput side in real numbers
docs.text: Level 4, Lesson 1 measured real producer throughput varying from roughly 41,000 to 88,000 records/sec depending purely on compression codec choice, on one laptop's worth of CPU. That's the real, concrete shape of the tradeoff self-managed infrastructure gives you direct control over: you can choose none for raw speed, accept gzip's throughput cost for smaller storage and network bills, or benchmark your own workload (as Lesson 1's own surprising lz4-latency result showed is necessary) rather than trusting a number from documentation. A managed service abstracts this choice into a pricing tier, but doesn't remove the underlying tradeoff — your actual bytes still have to be compressed, stored, and replicated somewhere, by someone's CPU and disk.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Self-managed Kafka's real cost structure is: infrastructure (the actual compute/disk this course's lab used, scaled up) plus operational labor — the actual, nontrivial work this entire course demonstrated by hand: formatting and configuring brokers (Level 1, Lesson 2), diagnosing a real broker failure (Level 1, Lesson 7; Level 4, Lesson 3), setting up security (Level 2, Lesson 7), running reassignments (Level 2, Lesson 8), and so on. Every one of those hands-on lessons represents real engineering time a self-managed deployment needs someone to actually do, repeatedly, as the cluster grows and changes — that labor cost is real, even though it doesn't show up on an infrastructure invoice the way a managed service's bill does.

Managed Kafka (Confluent Cloud, Amazon MSK, and similar) prices in that operational labor as part of the per-unit cost — you're paying, in effect, for someone else to have already built the automation this course's Level 4, Lesson 8 described Strimzi doing, plus a team on call for exactly the failure scenarios Lesson 3's real broker-kill test demonstrated. The crossover point — where self-managed's lower raw infrastructure cost stops winning against managed's lower labor cost — depends heavily on how much of this course's hands-on material (replication tuning, security configuration, failure diagnosis, capacity planning) your team would otherwise need to learn and maintain expertise in internally, which is a real, if hard-to-put-a-single-number- on, cost.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Comparing only the sticker price of infrastructure vs. a managed service's bill, ignoring the real operational labor self-managed Kafka requires — every "how do I..." this course answered by hand is a real skill someone on a self-managed team needs to have, continuously, not just once at setup time.
  • Assuming managed Kafka removes the need to understand Kafka's own concepts. As Lesson 8 covered for Kubernetes/Strimzi specifically, a managed service still requires understanding replication, partitioning, and consumer group behavior to use correctly and diagnose problems — it changes who operates the infrastructure, not what you need to know about the system itself.
  • Sizing a cost comparison off of throughput or storage estimates instead of a real benchmark. As this level's own lz4-latency surprise (Lesson 1) and per-record overhead measurement (Lesson 2) showed directly, real numbers on your actual workload can differ meaningfully from generic estimates — and that difference translates directly into cost at scale.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Using this level's real measured numbers (storage overhead from Lesson 2, throughput from Lesson 1) as a starting point, estimate the steady-state storage and the minimum broker capacity your own hypothetical workload (pick a real or plausible daily ingest volume) would need. Then separately estimate, honestly, how many hours per month a team would spend on the operational tasks this course demonstrated by hand (security setup, failure diagnosis, reassignment, upgrades) — and decide, with both real numbers in hand, where your own crossover point between self-managed and managed would actually sit.

docs.title: 10 · Capstone: Build, Break & Diagnose a Small Event-Driven Pipeline
docs.text: This capstone combines Levels 1 through 4: a real topic, real production traffic, a real broker failure with a consequence this course hasn't shown before — genuine, unrecoverable data unavailability — and the real, sometimes confusing client-side symptoms that failure produces.

docs.title: Build: a real topic, real traffic, spread across three brokers
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --topic capstone-orders --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic capstone-orders --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
Partition: 0  Leader: 2  Replicas: 2
Partition: 1  Leader: 3  Replicas: 3
Partition: 2  Leader: 1  Replicas: 1

$ bin/kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic capstone-orders --num-records 300 --record-size 100 ...
300 records sent, 1370 records/sec (0.13 MB/sec), ...

(Real output from this course's 3-broker lab cluster.) Deliberately replication factor 1 — each partition lives on exactly one broker, with no follower at all. This is the setup, and the choice, that makes this capstone's fault genuinely different from every earlier broker-kill test in this course, which always had real replicas to fail over to.

docs.title: Fault: killing the sole replica of a partition
docs.text:
$ kill -9 <broker-2-pid>

$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic capstone-orders --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
Partition: 0  Leader: none  Replicas: 2  Isr:  Elr: 2  LastKnownElr: 2
Partition: 1  Leader: 3     Replicas: 3  Isr: 3
Partition: 2  Leader: 1     Replicas: 1  Isr: 1

$ bin/kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic capstone-orders --partitions 0
(hangs — no response after 8+ seconds)

(Real output — a genuine kill -9, and a genuine client hang, not a staged timeout.) Partition 0's Leader is literally none — there is no other replica for the controller to fail over to, so this partition is offline, not degraded. Elr/LastKnownElr (eligible-leader tracking, a real KRaft 4.x metadata field) still remembers broker 2 was the last known leader, but that's informational, not a path to recovery while broker 2 stays down. Querying just that one partition's offsets doesn't return a clean error — it hangs, because the client is waiting for a leader response that will never come until the broker is actually restarted. Partitions 1 and 2, on different, still-healthy brokers, were completely unaffected the entire time.

docs.title: Diagnosing consumer-side impact
docs.text:
$ bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group capstone-group --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
GROUP           TOPIC            PARTITION  LOG-END-OFFSET  CONSUMER-ID
capstone-group  capstone-orders  0          0
capstone-group  capstone-orders  1          297
capstone-group  capstone-orders  2          4

(Real output.) LOG-END-OFFSET for partition 0 reads 0 — not because nothing was ever sent there, but because the perf-test producer's own partitioner, running during the outage window, simply routed around the unreachable partition for records it could still get acknowledged quickly, landing almost everything on partitions 1 and 2 instead. A consumer group describe here tells you the shape of the damage precisely: two healthy, actively-progressing partitions, and one that's silently received nothing, which is exactly the pattern worth distinguishing from "the whole topic is down" in a real incident.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Replication factor 1 isn't a lesser version of replication factor 3 — it's no replication at all, and this capstone's fault is the direct, real consequence: without a follower, there is nothing for the controller to promote when the sole replica dies, so the partition becomes genuinely offline rather than merely losing redundancy (contrast directly with Level 1, Lesson 7's replication-factor-3 kill, which kept serving throughout). The client-side hang, rather than a clean error, happens because the request genuinely has no answer to give yet — the client's metadata correctly shows no leader, and depending on the specific operation and its timeout configuration, it can wait rather than fail fast, which is itself a real, sometimes frustrating operational characteristic worth knowing rather than being surprised by during a real incident.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running replication factor 1 anywhere data loss or unavailability isn't acceptable, exactly the setup this capstone deliberately used to make its point concretely rather than just stating it.
  • Treating a hanging client request as "the whole cluster is down." As shown, two-thirds of this topic's partitions, on different brokers, kept working the entire time — a hang on one specific partition query is much more localized than it can feel like in the moment.
  • Assuming Elr/LastKnownElr metadata means automatic recovery is coming. It's a record of history, not an active failover path — the only real fix for an offline, unreplicated partition is getting its one true replica's broker back online.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this capstone's exact setup: a replication-factor-1 topic spread across a multi-broker cluster, real production traffic, then kill the broker holding one specific partition. Confirm that partition shows Leader: none and that querying it specifically hangs rather than erroring cleanly, while the other partitions remain completely unaffected. Then restart the broker and confirm the partition recovers — and compare the entire experience against Level 1, Lesson 7's replication-factor-3 version of the same kill, to make the real cost of skipping replication concrete in your own hands, not just in theory.
